docs.title: peabiru
docs.text:
peabiru computes travel-time matrices and accessibility on multimodal transport networks (walking, cycling, driving and public transport) built from an OpenStreetMap extract and GTFS feeds. It is a Rust port of Conveyal's R5 routing engine.

Authorship. peabiru is an independent project. Its routing model is that of Conveyal's R5, and its fare calculator and parts of its trip planner are translated from r5r (Ipea); both are MIT-licensed, and their notices are kept in LICENSE-THIRD-PARTY. peabiru is not affiliated with or endorsed by Conveyal, Ipea or the r5r team. The port was written with the assistance of AI coding tools.

The routing engine is written in Rust and runs inside the Python process: no Java is needed, the network is built once in memory and reused by every call, and results come back as pandas.DataFrames. The same Rust core powers the R package of the same name, with the same functions and arguments. See also the comparison with r5r.

Function What it computes build_network() a network from a directory with one .pbf and any GTFS .zip travel_time_matrix() travel times between every origin and destination accessibility() cumulative or decay-weighted access to opportunities expanded_travel_time_matrix() travel times minute by minute, with a breakdown of each trip arrival_travel_time_matrix() the latest trip that arrives by a given time isochrone() the areas or street segments reached within each cutoff detailed_itineraries() the legs of each trip, with their lines setup_fare_structure(), pareto_frontier() transit fares, and the trade-off between travel time and fare find_snap(), street_network_to_sf(), ... where points snap, the streets, stops and routes of a network get_gtfs_errors() the errors of the GTFS feeds

docs.title: Install
docs.text:
peabiru needs Python 3.9 or later; its only required dependency is pandas. Install geopandas as well to pass points as a GeoDataFrame.

pip install peabiru
pip install "peabiru[geo]"     # with geopandas

Wheels are built for Linux with glibc (x86_64 and aarch64), macOS (arm64 and x86_64) and Windows (x64). On Linux with musl (Alpine) and on Windows on Arm, pip builds the package from the source distribution, which needs a Rust toolchain (rustc 1.81 or later).

From a clone of the repository, with a Rust toolchain and maturin:

cd python
maturin develop --uv --release

docs.title: Get started
docs.text:
peabiru ships a small network for examples and tests: the streets around Avenida Paulista, in Sao Paulo, with the frequency-based GTFS feed of SPTrans. Build a network from its directory:

import peabiru

network = peabiru.build_network(peabiru.sample_data_path(), n_threads=2)
print(network.info())

{'vertices': 2609, 'edges': 5518, 'elevation': 'NONE', 'feeds': ['spo_gtfs'], 'stops': 654, 'patterns': 36, 'services': 6, 'frequencies': True}

print(network) shows the same summary, with the data path.

The network lives in memory and is reused by every routing call. Origins and destinations are pandas.DataFrames with columns id, lon and lat (in WGS 84); the sample comes with 27 points of a hexagonal grid:

points = peabiru.sample_points()

ttm = peabiru.travel_time_matrix(network, points, points, mode="WALK", n_threads=2)

ttm = peabiru.travel_time_matrix(
    network, points, points,
    mode=["WALK", "TRANSIT"],
    departure_datetime=dt.datetime(2019, 5, 13, 14, 0),
    percentiles=[25, 50, 75],
    seed=42,
    n_threads=2,
)

docs.title: What peabiru refuses
docs.text: A request peabiru does not support is an error that says so, never silently ignored: a fare structure that names a fare calculator (a type) instead of fare rules, expanded or arrival matrices by a street mode alone and pareto_frontier() with output_dir raise UnsupportedError; some elevation rasters, more than one .pbf file and a few itinerary pairs are errors too. The guides say where each of them applies.

docs.title: Sample data
docs.text: The sample network in peabiru.sample_data_path() is cut from the Sao Paulo sample data of the r5r project. spo_osm.pbf contains map data © OpenStreetMap contributors, available under the Open Database License; spo_gtfs.zip is a GTFS feed of SPTrans, without shapes.txt.

docs.title: Accessibility
docs.text:
accessibility() counts the opportunities (jobs, schools, people...) that can be reached from each origin, either within cutoffs or weighted by a decay function of the travel time.

import datetime as dt

import peabiru

network = peabiru.build_network(peabiru.sample_data_path(), n_threads=2)
points = peabiru.sample_points()
monday = dt.datetime(2019, 5, 13, 14, 0)

docs.title: Cumulative opportunities
docs.text:
The default decay function, "step", counts the opportunities reachable within each cutoff. The opportunity counts are numeric columns of destinations, named in opportunities_colnames:

access = peabiru.accessibility(
    network, points, points,
    opportunities_colnames=["jobs", "schools"],
    mode=["WALK", "TRANSIT"],
    departure_datetime=monday,
    cutoffs=[30, 15],
    percentiles=[50, 25],
    seed=42,
    n_threads=2,
)
print(access.head(8))
print(access.dtypes)

                id opportunity  percentile  cutoff  accessibility
0  89a8100c00fffff        jobs          25      15        12452.0
1  89a8100c00fffff        jobs          25      30        95249.0
2  89a8100c00fffff        jobs          50      15        12452.0
3  89a8100c00fffff        jobs          50      30        95249.0
4  89a8100c00fffff     schools          25      15            1.0
5  89a8100c00fffff     schools          25      30            4.0
6  89a8100c00fffff     schools          50      15            1.0
7  89a8100c00fffff     schools          50      30            4.0
id                object
opportunity       object
percentile         int32
cutoff             int32
accessibility    float64
dtype: object

There is one row per origin, opportunity, percentile and cutoff, in that order: origins and opportunities as given, percentiles and cutoffs ascending. Missing opportunity counts count as zero, with a warning.

With the "step" function, trips longer than the largest cutoff are not considered (max_trip_duration becomes max(cutoffs)), and max_trip_duration may never be shorter than the largest cutoff.

docs.title: Decay functions
docs.text:
The other functions weight each opportunity by its travel time. Their parameter is decay_value:

decay_function cutoffs decay_value "step" required None "exponential" required (each cutoff is a half-life) None "linear" required the width in minutes, a whole number from 1 to 59 "logistic" required the standard deviation in minutes, at least 1 "fixed_exponential" None the decay constant, between 0 and 1 
for fun, value in [("exponential", None), ("linear", 10), ("logistic", 5)]:
    a = peabiru.accessibility(
        network, points, points,
        opportunities_colnames="jobs",
        mode="WALK",
        decay_function=fun,
        decay_value=value,
        cutoffs=20,
        n_threads=2,
    )
    print(f"{fun:12s} {float(a['accessibility'].iloc[0])!r}")

exponential  42932.32347019101
linear       18205.424166666664
logistic     20362.754369823153

"fixed_exponential" has no cutoff, so the result has no cutoff column:

a = peabiru.accessibility(
    network, points, points,
    opportunities_colnames="jobs",
    mode="BICYCLE",
    decay_function="fixed_exponential",
    decay_value=0.002,
    n_threads=2,
)
print(a.head(3))

                id opportunity  percentile  accessibility
0  89a8100c00fffff        jobs          50   24448.202280
1  89a8100c007ffff        jobs          50   21875.710706
2  89a8100c077ffff        jobs          50   24385.802656

Accessibility values are doubles (float64). The travel time given to the decay function is the percentile in seconds, not rounded to minutes, and the exponential is table-based (a translation of Apache Commons Math's FastMath.exp()) rather than the C library's, so the values do not depend on the platform's maths library.

docs.title: Street modes
docs.text:
With "WALK", "BICYCLE" or "CAR" alone, each destination has one travel time, so every percentile gets the same value. departure_datetime is then not needed.

by_car = peabiru.accessibility(
    network, points, points,
    opportunities_colnames="population",
    mode="CAR",
    cutoffs=[5, 10],
    n_threads=2,
)
wide = by_car.pivot(index="id", columns="cutoff", values="accessibility")
print(wide.head(3))

id

docs.title: Compared with r5r and r5py
docs.text: r5r is the R interface to R5, Conveyal's routing engine in Java, developed at Ipea; r5py is a Python wrapper of the same engine. peabiru is an independent package with an engine of its own, written in Rust. This is the one page of the documentation that compares them: what peabiru shares with r5r, where it differs, and how to move a script over.

docs.title: What is shared
docs.text:
• The routing model. peabiru's engine is a port of R5 7.6, the version r5r 2.5.0 runs: the street network built from OpenStreetMap, the transit layer built from GTFS, the searches, the Monte Carlo draws of frequency-based feeds, the decay functions, the fare router.
  • The fine print of the model. Details that other pages state as plain facts about peabiru are R5's: the multi-criteria router (McRAPTOR) used with fares and for alternative itineraries, and its sampling of departure times; the fare rules (R5's rule-based in-routing fare calculator), with fares read as 32-bit floats; the levels of traffic stress; the limits (5,000 destinations for the expanded and arrival matrices, egress searched up to 5 km by bicycle or 30 minutes by car); elevations in 16-bit decimetres and car speeds in 16-bit centimetres per second; the checks of the GTFS feeds (those of gtfs-lib, R5's GTFS library); and the numbers in the files of output_dir, written as Java writes a double (2.0, 1.0E-4).
  • The vocabulary. The functions peabiru has in common with r5r have the same names, and their arguments the same names, order and defaults, apart from the items listed below.
  • The results. For the same call, peabiru and r5r 2.5.0 return the same rows, in the same order, with the same values, including the last bit of the accessibility values. This is checked in peabiru's repository, not assumed: bench/compare/py_parity.py runs 130 calls through both packages on r5r's two sample cities (Porto Alegre and Sao Paulo) and compares every value; bench/compare/py_output_dir.py compares the files written with output_dir byte for byte (151 files); bench/compare/py_formals.py compares the arguments and defaults of every function (209 arguments); and bench/compare/py_argument_errors.py checks the cases of invalid arguments shared by the R, Python and JavaScript packages. On the larger examples of this documentation the two also agree where they were compared: in Recife, the 17 cells of Boa Viagem without a car route have none in r5r 2.5.0 either, and in the fares analysis of Porto Alegre, on 103 origins, r5r 2.5.0 gives the same access as peabiru, origin by origin, with the fare structure and without it.

Besides the functions it shares with r5r, peabiru has functions of its own, which r5r has not: trip_options(), and locate_facilities() and floating_catchment().

docs.title: Moving a script from r5r
docs.text:
Calls translate one to one; the R types become Python types, and r5r's r5r_network argument is called network.

r5r (R) peabiru (Python) r5r_network <- build_network(path) network = peabiru.build_network(path) travel_time_matrix(r5r_network, origins, destinations, ...) peabiru.travel_time_matrix(network, origins, destinations, ...) travel_time_matrix(r5r_network = net, ...) peabiru.travel_time_matrix(network=net, ...) setup_r5(), stop_r5(), download_r5(), r5r_cache(), r5r_sitrep(), options(java.parameters = ...) nothing: there is no Java to set up, stop or give memory to data.frame / sf POINT with id, lon, lat pandas.DataFrame with id, lon, lat / geopandas.GeoDataFrame of points mode = c("WALK", "TRANSIT") mode=["WALK", "TRANSIT"] (or a string) departure_datetime = as.POSIXct("2019-05-13 14:00:00", tz = "America/Sao_Paulo") departure_datetime=datetime.datetime(2019, 5, 13, 14, 0) (naive or aware) max_walk_time = Inf, n_threads = Inf max_walk_time=math.inf, n_threads=math.inf (the default; None means the same) NULL (seed, cutoffs, decay_value, ...) None c(0, 15, 30) (cutoffs, percentiles, ...) a list or tuple, [0, 15, 30] result data.table / sf result pandas.DataFrame / geopandas.GeoDataFrame integer columns with NA (travel_time_pXX, n_rides, travel_time) nullable Int32 with <NA> integer columns without NA (percentile, cutoff, draw_number, option, segment, ...) int32 double columns (accessibility, times of expanded matrices, ...) float64, NaN where r5r has NA double OpenStreetMap ids (osm_id of street_network_to_sf() and line isochrones) int64 (R has no 64-bit integers) character columns (from_id, to_id, id, opportunity, departure_time, routes, ...) object dtype holding str; a missing value is None logical columns (found, walk, car, ...) bool Date column of check_transit_availability() datetime64 a fare structure (a list of settings and data.tables) a dict with the same keys, and pandas.DataFrame tables street_network_bbox(output = "bbox") / "vector" / "polygon" a tuple (xmin, ymin, xmax, ymax) / a dict with those keys / a GeoSeries

For example, this r5r call

ttm <- travel_time_matrix(
  r5r_network, points, points,
  mode = c("WALK", "TRANSIT"),
  departure_datetime = as.POSIXct("2019-05-13 14:00:00", tz = "America/Sao_Paulo"),
  percentiles = c(25, 75),
  max_walk_time = 15,
  seed = 42
)

is, in peabiru:

import datetime as dt
import peabiru

network = peabiru.build_network(peabiru.sample_data_path(), n_threads=2)
points = peabiru.sample_points()
ttm = peabiru.travel_time_matrix(
    network, points, points,
    mode=["WALK", "TRANSIT"],
    departure_datetime=dt.datetime(2019, 5, 13, 14, 0),
    percentiles=[25, 75],
    max_walk_time=15,
    seed=42,
    n_threads=2,
)
print(ttm.dtypes)

from_id            object
to_id              object
travel_time_p25     Int32
travel_time_p75     Int32
dtype: object

docs.title: General
docs.text:
• No Java. There is no JVM, no java.parameters and no R5 jar. r5r's five functions that manage Java (setup_r5(), stop_r5(), download_r5(), r5r_cache(), r5r_sitrep()) do not exist in peabiru: there is nothing to manage.
  • Argument names. r5r's r5r_network is network in peabiru. r5r's deprecated arguments do not exist: r5r_core (its old name for the network argument) and isochrone(sample_size=...).
  • Results are pandas objects: pandas.DataFrames, and geopandas.GeoDataFrames where r5r returns sf objects (also the tables of a fare structure and the edges, vertices, stops and routes of the network). Column names, order and values are the same; the types are the Python equivalents in the table above.
  • Geometries in another coordinate reference system (R only). The R package of peabiru reprojects an sf input in any CRS to WGS 84, with a message, where r5r stops with an error. In Python, as in r5r, a GeoDataFrame of points or of scenario polygons or lines must be in EPSG:4326 (a ValueError otherwise): reproject it with GeoDataFrame.to_crs(4326).
  • The network lives in memory only. Nothing is written to the data directory (r5r writes network.dat and gtfs_errors.csv there); a Network cannot be pickled and is built again in each process (it takes seconds even for a whole city). overwrite and temp_dir are accepted and checked, and have no effect.
  • build_network() takes n_threads, the threads used to read the .pbf.
  • verbose and progress are checked, but peabiru prints no progress counter; verbose=True only reports the build of the network, on standard error.
  • Errors are Python exceptions, with messages of peabiru's own. The checks of the arguments are the same as r5r's, and most messages read as r5r's (checkmate's and cli's wording) in Python's terms: None for NULL, bool, str, float, int and datetime for R's types, positions counted from 1 as in R, cli's bullets and line breaks dropped, network and peabiru.Network where the network is named. Some are worded differently: r5r turns numbers and logical values given as a mode (mode, mode_egress, by) into text and reports the text as not a mode, where Python reports the value's type; arrival_datetime is checked itself (r5r checks the departure, arrival_datetime - max_trip_duration); all_to_all is named as such (r5r names the internal unique_ids); and a missing fare_cutoffs is the default. The repository checks the 1,367 cases shared by the three packages (bench/compare/argument_errors.json): 1,215 read the same in Python, and 152 are the ones worded differently. Classes: TypeError for an argument of the wrong type, ValueError for an invalid value, RuntimeError for a file that cannot be read or a network that cannot be built, and peabiru.UnsupportedError (a NotImplementedError) for the refusals listed below. Warnings (ids that are not strings, missing coordinates, missing opportunity counts, few services running on the date, ...) are UserWarnings.

docs.title: Where peabiru is deterministic and r5r is not
docs.text:
• get_gtfs_errors() reads the feeds again (r5r reads the gtfs_errors.csv its build_network() wrote) and lists the rows feed by feed in the order gtfs-lib finds them; r5r's order is that of a Java HashSet and changes from run to run. The rows and columns are the same.
  • Elevation rasters in a projected system. In a raster that is not in EPSG:4326, r5r reads one pixel or the other for a street point within nanometres (5e-8 m, or 2e-13 degrees) of a pixel boundary or of the raster's edge, depending on the last bits of the JVM's sines and cosines; peabiru reads the pixel Java's StrictMath gives, on every machine, and warns once with the number of such points (see Elevation).
  • Expanded and arrival matrices need public transport. With a street mode alone, r5r reports the same trip for every minute of a departure time taken from the computer's clock, not from departure_datetime; peabiru raises UnsupportedError there (use travel_time_matrix() for street modes).

Not a difference: without seed, frequency-based GTFS feeds give random results in both packages; with a seed, the draws are the same.

docs.title: Warnings peabiru adds
docs.text: • Voids and out-of-range elevations. Voids and values beyond +/-3276.7 m are stored wrapped around in both packages (R5 keeps decimetres in 16-bit integers: SRTM's -32768 voids become 0 m, -9999 becomes 3108.2 m, and a NaN no-data value is stored as 0 m), so the slope costs are the same; peabiru warns, counting them and the samples equal to the raster's no-data value. r5r is silent. (The StrictMath item above also warns.) r5r warns on every call with a scenario that walking and cycling may be affected by missing elevation; peabiru warns, in its own words, only on a network with elevation.

docs.title: Errors where r5r fails later or routes on corrupted values
docs.text:
• Clear errors instead of failures. peabiru raises an error of its own, saying what is wrong, where r5r lets a value through and then fails in Java or with an internal R error: an empty percentiles; a missing destination id, or any missing id with output_dir (Java's NullPointerException); an arrival_datetime that is not a datetime; an isochrone polygon_output that is not a boolean, or a fractional zoom (r5r passes it to R5); origins without rows in isochrone(); a carspeed_scale of NaN; an osm_id, max_speed or lts of a scenario table that Java cannot parse (NumberFormatException); a zero-length radius in find_snap(); a fare structure with a column r5r does not know, whose fare type is not in fares_per_type or that misses a route of the network (Java's NullPointerException); write_fare_structure() on a structure that is not one; get_gtfs_errors() on a folder that does not exist.
  • Scenarios R5 would corrupt. Scenarios whose car speeds R5's 16-bit cm/s would wrap or bring to 0 or less (a negative factor or speed in new_carspeeds, a polygon scale of math.inf or 0, a carspeed_scale far above 1) and a carspeed_scale beyond the 32-bit float range are errors; r5r routes on the wrapped speeds, hands R5 Infinity, or fails dividing by zero. Polygons that are not valid, and ties between polygons that peabiru cannot settle exactly as R5 does, are errors too (see Scenarios).

docs.title: Refusals
docs.text:
r5r accepts these; peabiru stops with an error that says so, never ignoring the request:

  • R5's own fare calculators (a fare structure with a type): UnsupportedError.
  • An elevation raster that is not a one-band GeoTIFF, north up, uncompressed or compressed with LZW, Deflate or PackBits, in EPSG:4326 or in a system whose GeoTools transform peabiru reproduces (SIRGAS 2000 4674, SAD69 4618, Corrego Alegre 4225 and their UTM zones used in Brazil, SIRGAS 2000 / Brazil Polyconic 5880, WGS 84 / UTM 32601-32660 and 32701-32760, Pseudo-Mercator 3857) given by its EPSG code; a .prj file next to the raster (r5r uses its system instead of the GeoTIFF's); a raster named .tiff (r5r fails on it); more than one raster in the data directory (r5r reads the last one listed); a street point that StrictMath puts on a projected raster's outer edge (r5r fails there too). These are RuntimeErrors from build_network().
  • More than one .pbf file in the data directory (r5r uses one of them): ValueError.
  • Ids that cannot name a file, with output_dir. The files are named after the ids (from_<id>.csv), so an id holding a path separator (/ or \) or NUL, and on Windows also < > : " | ? *, raises ValueError naming the id, before anything is routed or written. r5r fails on such an id with Java's FileNotFoundException (a/b, ../x) or writes a file of another name (from_a\b.csv on Linux and macOS). trip_options() follows the same rule; detailed_itineraries() keeps the check r5r makes.
  • pareto_frontier() with output_dir (r5r writes CSV files): UnsupportedError.
  • detailed_itineraries() with mode_egress="CAR": where a car search crosses a turn restriction with two or more via ways, r5r's itineraries can depend on the searches that ran before (R5 reverses those via edges in place); peabiru returns what r5r gives on a freshly built network for that pair alone with one thread, with a warning naming the pairs some other order would change (see Detailed itineraries). In r5r a car matrix, accessibility or Pareto frontier computed after such a call could differ too (none did on Porto Alegre); peabiru's are those of a fresh network.

(The expanded and arrival matrices by a street mode alone, above, are also a refusal.)

docs.title: Output details
docs.text:
• write_fare_structure() writes the same CSV files as r5r, deflated in the same order, but the archive's bytes differ from r5r's (which also holds file dates); each package reads the other's files. As in r5r 2.5.0, debug_path and debug_info are kept in the structure and no debug file is written.
  • isochrone() returns the polygons r5r hands to sf::st_make_valid(), vertex for vertex on the same platform, without that last s2 rebuild: they cover the same areas but are not snapped to 1e-7 degrees and are always MultiPolygons. Pass them to shapely.make_valid() if your tools need valid geometries. Line isochrones route to the centroids r5r takes with sf::st_centroid(), to within about 1e-14 degrees.
  • Not a difference, but worth knowing: GTFS feeds are loaded in the order in which the operating system lists the directory, as R5 loads them, so with more than one feed the expanded and arrival matrices can differ slightly between macOS and Linux (another stop or route for a few trips), exactly as r5r's do; isochrone rings follow the C++ library isoband is built with (libc++ on macOS, libstdc++ on Linux and Windows), as r5r's.

docs.title: Only in Python
docs.text:
• Required arguments after optional ones have a default of None (Python cannot have a required argument after optional ones): arrival_datetime of arrival_travel_time_matrix(), and fare_structure and fare_cutoffs of pareto_frontier(). Leaving them out is an error, as in r5r.
  • Ids that are not strings are converted with str(), with a warning, as r5r converts them. For integer ids this is what R's as.character() gives; for floating-point ids the text can differ (str(1.0) is "1.0", R gives "1").
  • Naive datetimes are read as clock times. For arrival_travel_time_matrix(), arrival_datetime - max_trip_duration is then computed on the clock time; an aware datetime gets R's POSIXct arithmetic on the absolute time (which matters only across a daylight-saving change).
  • A route of transit_network_to_sf() whose line has a single point (a pattern with one linked stop) is a shapely Point; r5r's sf holds a one-point LINESTRING, which shapely cannot represent.

docs.title: The same on purpose
docs.text:
Some behaviours that may surprise are R5's or r5r's, and peabiru has them too, so that the results are equal:

  • walking trips are routed from the destinations when there are more origins than destinations (and no elevation raster), and the columns swapped back;
  • the Monte Carlo draws of frequency-based feeds come from R5's random number generator (a Mersenne Twister seeded from seed and the origin's coordinates), so the same seed gives the same numbers;
  • accessibility uses the FastMath.exp() of Apache Commons Math that R5 calls, which makes the values bit-identical;
  • departure times past midnight are written past 24:00:00, as R5 writes them, and the expanded and arrival matrices accept at most 5,000 destinations, R5's limit;
  • max_lts defaults to 2 and max_rides to 3;
  • CAR_PARK and BICYCLE_RENT are rejected;
  • build_network() refuses a GTFS feed with errors of priority HIGH;
  • detailed_itineraries() refuses public transport on a network with frequency-based trips, numbers the options in the same order, and gives the same OpenStreetMap ids with osm_link_ids=True;
  • with fares, exactly 200 Monte Carlo draws, or too many for the window, are errors (r5r issue 602);
  • a call with a scenario routes without slope costs (r5r issue 555).

docs.title: From r5py
docs.text:
r5py has an API of its own. The main correspondences, with r5py's names as of r5py 1.1.7:

(minutes) speed_walking=3.6, speed_cycling=12.0 walk_speed=3.6, bike_speed=12 max_bicycle_traffic_stress (default 3) max_lts (default 2) max_public_transport_rides (default 8) max_rides (default 3) result column travel_time (with the default percentiles=[50]) travel_time_p50 (always one column per percentile) TransportNetwork(..., elevation_model="dem.tif", elevation_cost_function=ElevationCostFunction.TOBLER) a .tif raster in the directory and build_network(directory, elevation="TOBLER") (see Elevation) DetailedItineraries(network, origins, destinations, force_all_to_all=True, ...) detailed_itineraries(network, origins, destinations, all_to_all=True, ...) Isochrones(network, origins, isochrones=[timedelta(minutes=15), ...], ...) isochrone(network, origins, cutoffs=[15, ...], ...) (minutes)

Results are equal to r5py's only where r5py runs the same R5 version with the same parameters; peabiru is compared with r5r, not with r5py.

docs.title: Elevation
docs.text:
A .tif elevation raster in the data directory gives walking and cycling times slope costs: build_network() samples the raster every 10 m along each street, at the nearest pixel, and multiplies the time of each street by the average cost of its slopes (the parts of streets at the origin and the destination keep their plain times). Car times never change. The cost function is chosen with elevation:

  • "TOBLER" (the default): Tobler's hiking function;
  • "MINETTI": Minetti's energy cost of walking on slopes;
  • "NONE": no slope costs, even with a raster.

The examples use the sample network with three small synthetic rasters made for the package's tests (smooth hills between 743 and 834 m over the sample area, not measured data), downloaded once into the temporary directory (about 9 kB):

import shutil
import tempfile
import urllib.request
import warnings
from pathlib import Path

import peabiru

raw = ("https://raw.githubusercontent.com/StrategicProjects/peabiru-routing/"
       "7184f3f2fdadc4cf05ede19d832f2ad5606be712/python/tests/data/")
rasters = Path(tempfile.gettempdir()) / "peabiru-rasters"
rasters.mkdir(exist_ok=True)
for name in ["spo_hills.tif", "spo_hills_31983.tif", "spo_voids.tif"]:
    if not (rasters / name).exists():
        urllib.request.urlretrieve(raw + name, rasters / name)


def data_dir(raster=None, name="hills.tif"):
    """A new directory with the sample .pbf and GTFS feed, and a raster."""
    d = Path(tempfile.mkdtemp())
    for f in ["spo_osm.pbf", "spo_gtfs.zip"]:
        shutil.copy(Path(peabiru.sample_data_path()) / f, d)
    if raster is not None:
        shutil.copy(rasters / raster, d / name)
    return d


points = peabiru.sample_points()

docs.title: Slope costs
docs.text:
The same directory, built with each cost function:

hills = data_dir("spo_hills.tif")
networks = {e: peabiru.build_network(hills, elevation=e, n_threads=2)
            for e in ["NONE", "TOBLER", "MINETTI"]}
print({e: n.elevation for e, n in networks.items()})

{'NONE': 'NONE', 'TOBLER': 'TOBLER', 'MINETTI': 'MINETTI'}

The mean travel time between the 27 sample points, by mode and cost function:

import pandas as pd

rows = {}
for e, network in networks.items():
    rows[e] = {
        mode: peabiru.travel_time_matrix(network, points, points, mode=mode, n_threads=2)
        ["travel_time_p50"].astype(float).mean().round(2)
        for mode in ["WALK", "BICYCLE", "CAR"]
    }
print(pd.DataFrame(rows).T)

          WALK  BICYCLE   CAR
NONE     19.70    11.82  7.46
TOBLER   20.40    12.17  7.46
MINETTI  21.06    12.46  7.46

network.elevation tells which function a network uses. Without any .tif file in the directory the network is built with "NONE", whatever elevation says; as with the .pbf and the GTFS feeds, only a lower-case extension counts (a HILLS.TIF is ignored).

docs.title: Rasters in other coordinate systems
docs.text:
The raster must be a one-band GeoTIFF, north up, uncompressed or compressed with LZW, Deflate or PackBits (what GDAL writes by default). Besides WGS 84 longitude and latitude (EPSG:4326), peabiru reads the systems whose transform it reproduces exactly, given by their EPSG code (what GDAL writes): SIRGAS 2000 (4674), SAD69 (4618), Corrego Alegre 1970-72 (4225), their UTM zones used in Brazil, SIRGAS 2000 / Brazil Polyconic (5880), WGS 84 / UTM (32601-32660, 32701-32760) and WGS 84 / Pseudo-Mercator (3857). The same hills in SIRGAS 2000 / UTM zone 23S (EPSG:31983):

utm = peabiru.build_network(data_dir("spo_hills_31983.tif"), n_threads=2)
walk = peabiru.travel_time_matrix(utm, points, points, mode="WALK", n_threads=2)
print(utm.elevation, walk["travel_time_p50"].astype(float).mean().round(2))

TOBLER 20.38

The mean differs a little from the EPSG:4326 raster's (20.40): the reprojected pixels are not the same pixels.

docs.title: The same result on every machine
docs.text:
In a projected system, which pixel a street point falls in is computed with sines and cosines. For a point within nanometres (5e-8 m, or 2e-13 degrees) of the boundary between two pixels of different values, or of the raster's edge, the answer depends on the last bits of the trigonometry. peabiru computes it itself, bit for bit the same way, so it reads the same pixel on every machine, and warns once with the number of such points: about one in a hundred million for 30 m pixels. Reprojecting the raster to EPSG:4326 removes the ambiguity. The sample has none, so building it gives no warning:

with warnings.catch_warnings(record=True) as caught:
    warnings.simplefilter("always")
    peabiru.build_network(data_dir("spo_hills_31983.tif"), n_threads=2)
print(len(caught), "warnings")

0 warnings

A point that falls on the raster's outer edge (inside its envelope, past the last pixel) is an error: there is no pixel to read.

docs.title: Voids and out-of-range values
docs.text:
Elevations are kept in decimetres in 16-bit integers. Voids and values beyond +/-3276.7 m therefore wrap around: SRTM's -32768 voids become 0 m, -9999 becomes 3108.2 m, and a NaN no-data value is stored as 0 m. The slope costs are computed on the wrapped values; peabiru warns, counting such samples and those equal to the raster's no-data value. A raster with voids:

with warnings.catch_warnings(record=True) as caught:
    warnings.simplefilter("always")
    voids = peabiru.build_network(data_dir("spo_voids.tif"), n_threads=2)
for w in caught:
    print(w.category.__name__, w.message)

UserWarning of the 21899 elevation samples on the network, 6298 with a value beyond +/-3276.7 m, which is stored wrapped around as 16-bit decimetres (an SRTM void of -32768 becomes 0 m, -9999 becomes 3108.2 m, 3500 m becomes -3053.6 m); the slope costs follow from these values, and are probably not what you want there: fill the voids or crop the raster

Fill the voids (with gdal_fillnodata, for instance) or crop the raster to the study area before building the network.

docs.title: Rasters peabiru refuses
docs.text:
These are a RuntimeError that says what to change:

  • a .prj file next to the raster (it would contradict or duplicate the GeoTIFF's own coordinate system);
  • a raster whose name ends in .tiff (rename it to .tif);
  • more than one raster in the directory (which one to read would be arbitrary);
  • a raster in another coordinate system, or with another layout or compression.
d = data_dir("spo_hills.tif")
(d / "hills.prj").write_text("")
try:
    peabiru.build_network(d, n_threads=2)
except RuntimeError as e:
    print("RuntimeError:", str(e).split(": ", 1)[1][:60], "...")

RuntimeError: the raster has a hills.prj file next to it, whose coordinate ...

docs.title: Elevation and scenarios
docs.text:
A routing call with a scenario (new_carspeeds, carspeed_scale or new_lts, see Scenarios) runs on a copy of the network without the slope costs, with a warning:

tobler = networks["TOBLER"]
with warnings.catch_warnings(record=True) as caught:
    warnings.simplefilter("always")
    scenario = peabiru.travel_time_matrix(
        tobler, points, points, mode="WALK", carspeed_scale=0.8, n_threads=2
    )
print(caught[0].message)
flat = peabiru.travel_time_matrix(networks["NONE"], points, points, mode="WALK", n_threads=2)
print(scenario.equals(flat))

A scenario was used for this calculation: WALK and BICYCLE are routed without the slope costs of the network's elevation.
True

A network with elevation also turns off one shortcut: a walking matrix with more origins than destinations is routed from the destinations (and the columns swapped back) only when the data directory has no .tif file.

docs.title: Example: mapping access to jobs and schools
docs.text:
How many jobs can people reach from where they live? This example answers that for Porto Alegre, on a grid of hexagonal cells, first walking and then walking with public transport. The code blocks make one script; the output shown under each is what it prints. The map at the end needs matplotlib.

The accessibility computed below. This figure is drawn from the same results, in the style of these pages, by site/figures/figures.R in the repository.

docs.title: The data
docs.text:
The sample data of Porto Alegre from the r5r project (an OpenStreetMap extract, the bus and train GTFS feeds, and a grid of 1,227 hexagonal cells with their population, jobs and schools), downloaded once into the temporary directory:

import datetime as dt
import tempfile
import urllib.request
from pathlib import Path

import pandas as pd

import peabiru

poa = Path(tempfile.gettempdir()) / "peabiru-poa"
poa.mkdir(exist_ok=True)
url = "https://raw.githubusercontent.com/ipea/r5r/v2.5.0/r-package/inst/extdata/poa/"
for name in ["poa_osm.pbf", "poa_eptc.zip", "poa_trensurb.zip",
             "poa_hexgrid.csv", "poa_points_of_interest.csv"]:
    if not (poa / name).exists():
        urllib.request.urlretrieve(url + name, poa / name)

network = peabiru.build_network(poa)
grid = pd.read_csv(poa / "poa_hexgrid.csv")
print(grid.head().to_string())
print(grid[["population", "schools", "jobs"]].sum())

Each cell is a point at its centre. The bus feed of the sample only has trips between late morning and early evening on weekdays, so public transport is routed from 14:00 on a Monday, over a 30-minute window of departures:

monday = dt.datetime(2019, 5, 13, 14, 0)

docs.title: Travel times from one point
docs.text:
A first look: the travel time from one place, Farroupilha Park, to the centre of every cell. Pairs that take longer than max_trip_duration are left out of the result.

poi = pd.read_csv(poa / "poa_points_of_interest.csv")
park = poi[poi["id"] == "farroupilha_park"]

walk = peabiru.travel_time_matrix(network, park, grid, mode="WALK",
                                  max_trip_duration=60)
transit = peabiru.travel_time_matrix(
    network, park, grid, mode=["WALK", "TRANSIT"],
    departure_datetime=monday, time_window=30, max_trip_duration=60,
)
for label, ttm in [("walking", walk), ("public transport", transit)]:
    print(f"{label}: {len(ttm)} cells within an hour, "
          f"median {ttm['travel_time_p50'].median():.0f} min")

walking: 268 cells within an hour, median 41 min
public transport: 1100 cells within an hour, median 39 min

Within an hour, public transport reaches about four times as many cells as walking does.

docs.title: Jobs and schools within 30 minutes
docs.text:
accessibility() adds up, for each origin, the opportunities at every destination reached within the cutoff (the "step" decay function, the default). Five cells have no job count; they count as zero, with a warning.

import warnings

with warnings.catch_warnings():
    warnings.simplefilter("ignore")      # the five cells without a job count
    access = pd.concat([
        peabiru.accessibility(
            network, grid, grid, opportunities_colnames=["jobs", "schools"],
            mode="WALK", cutoffs=30,
        ).assign(mode="walking"),
        peabiru.accessibility(
            network, grid, grid, opportunities_colnames=["jobs", "schools"],
            mode=["WALK", "TRANSIT"], departure_datetime=monday,
            time_window=30, cutoffs=30,
        ).assign(mode="public transport"),
    ], ignore_index=True)
print(access.head())

                id opportunity  percentile  cutoff  accessibility     mode
0  89a901291abffff        jobs          50      30        15978.0  walking
1  89a901291abffff     schools          50      30           12.0  walking
2  89a9012a3cfffff        jobs          50      30          641.0  walking
3  89a9012a3cfffff     schools          50      30            0.0  walking
4  89a901295b7ffff        jobs          50      30         1884.0  walking

Weighting each cell by the people who live there gives what the average resident reaches:

access = access.merge(grid[["id", "population"]], on="id")
average = access.groupby(["mode", "opportunity"]).apply(
    lambda a: round((a["accessibility"] * a["population"]).sum() / a["population"].sum()),
    include_groups=False,
)
print(average.unstack())

opportunity        jobs  schools
mode                            
public transport  67725       31
walking           21343       12

Public transport roughly triples both: about 21 thousand jobs and 12 schools within half an hour on foot, against 68 thousand jobs and 31 schools with the buses and the train.

docs.title: A map
docs.text:
Each cell drawn as a dot at its centre, coloured by the jobs it reaches:

import matplotlib

matplotlib.use("Agg")
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

jobs = access[access["opportunity"] == "jobs"].merge(grid[["id", "lon", "lat"]], on="id")
fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(10, 5), sharex=True, sharey=True)
for ax, (label, cells) in zip(axes, jobs.groupby("mode", sort=False)):
    dots = ax.scatter(cells["lon"], cells["lat"], c=cells["accessibility"] / 1000,
                      s=9, cmap="Greens", vmin=0, vmax=200)
    ax.set_title(label, loc="left", fontweight="bold")
    ax.set_aspect(1 / 0.866)              # degrees of longitude are shorter at 30° S
    ax.set_axis_off()
fig.colorbar(dots, ax=axes, shrink=0.7, label="thousand jobs within 30 min")
fig.savefig("accessibility.png", dpi=110, bbox_inches="tight")

docs.title: Variations
docs.text:
• Gradual access. decay_function="logistic" (or "exponential", "linear", "fixed_exponential") weights every job by its travel time instead of counting those under a hard limit; see Accessibility.
  • Several cutoffs at once. cutoffs=[15, 30, 45] returns one row per cutoff, from a single routing pass.
  • Percentiles. With percentiles=[25, 50, 75], the accessibility of a good, a typical and a bad departure in the window.

docs.title: Example: who reaches the jobs in Belo Horizonte, and what a fare budget leaves
docs.text:
How many jobs can a resident reach in an hour by bus, and does the answer depend on how much the household earns? This example measures it for Belo Horizonte from the city's official GTFS feed, on the grid of Ipea's Access to Opportunities Project, and then, in Porto Alegre, asks what is left of that access when the fare is limited.

It is the Python half of a larger example: the R article does the same for São Paulo and Rio de Janeiro too, compares the three cities, and explains which capitals were left out and why. The numbers printed here for Belo Horizonte and Porto Alegre are the ones of that article; they were computed on 2026-11-12. It needs geopandas 1.0 or later and, to cut the extract, osmium.

The jobs within an hour by bus, computed below. The figures of this page are drawn from the same results by site/figures/capitals.R in the repository.

docs.title: The data
docs.text:
Data Source Licence Streets OpenStreetMap, extract of the Sudeste region by Geofabrik, dated 2026-11-01 (863 MB) ODbL 1.0 GTFS Superintendência de Mobilidade de Belo Horizonte (SUMOB), "GTFS": the conventional and the supplementary bus systems, by timetable; no metro. Version 202611111921 (52 MB); the address always serves the current file, rewritten every day CC BY Municipal boundary IBGE, malhas municipais (API, version 3) public data, IBGE Cells, population, income Ipea, Access to Opportunities Project, data release v1.0.0 of aopdata: H3 cells of resolution 9 with the residents and the household income per person of the Censo 2010 the aopdata repository is MIT; no separate licence for the data is stated. Ipea asks for the citations at the end of this page Jobs, schools, health facilities the same release, land use of 2019: formal jobs (RAIS), public schools, public health facilities, per cell same Porto Alegre the sample data of r5r 2.5.0: OpenStreetMap extract, GTFS of EPTC and Trensurb of May 2019, grid, and a fare structure r5r is under GPL (>= 3) or MIT, at the user's choice; map data ODbL

The public transport is of November 2026; the residents and their income are those of 2010 (the Censo 2022 has no income by census tract yet) and the jobs those of 2019.

import datetime as dt
import gzip
import hashlib
import os
import shutil
import subprocess
import urllib.request
import zipfile
from pathlib import Path

import geopandas as gpd
import numpy as np
import pandas as pd

import peabiru

data_dir = Path(os.environ.get("PEABIRU_EXAMPLE_DATA", "capitals-data"))
raw = data_dir / "raw"
raw.mkdir(parents=True, exist_ok=True)


def fetch(url, name=None, folder=raw):
    dest = folder / (name or url.rsplit("/", 1)[1])
    if not dest.exists():
        part = dest.with_suffix(".part")
        request = urllib.request.Request(url, headers={"User-Agent": "peabiru-docs-examples"})
        with urllib.request.urlopen(request) as response, open(part, "wb") as out:
            # IBGE's API sends its answer gzip-compressed, asked or not
            gz = response.headers.get("Content-Encoding") == "gzip"
            shutil.copyfileobj(gzip.GzipFile(fileobj=response) if gz else response, out)
        part.rename(dest)
    return dest


def aop(name):
    return fetch("https://github.com/ipeaGIT/aopdata/releases/download/v1.0.0/" + name)


sudeste = fetch("https://download.geofabrik.de/south-america/brazil/sudeste-261101.osm.pbf")
feed = fetch("https://s3.amazonaws.com/mobilibus-uploads/gtfs/GTFSBHTRANS.zip", "bhtrans.zip")
print(f"{feed.stat().st_size / 1e6:.1f} MB, sha256", hashlib.sha256(feed.read_bytes()).hexdigest()[:16])

52.2 MB, sha256 15d3b184fe8e1e3a

A later download is another version of the network and gives other numbers; the checksum (its first 16 digits) identifies the file used here.

docs.title: The network
docs.text:
The streets are cut around the municipality and the stops of the feed, with 3 km to spare; build_network() reads the directory with the cut and the feed.

utm = 31983   # SIRGAS 2000 / UTM zone 23S, in metres

boundary = gpd.read_file(fetch(
    "https://servicodados.ibge.gov.br/api/v3/malhas/municipios/3106200"
    "?formato=application/vnd.geo+json&qualidade=maxima", "3106200.geojson")).to_crs(utm)
with zipfile.ZipFile(feed) as z, z.open("stops.txt") as f:
    stops = pd.read_csv(f, usecols=["stop_lon", "stop_lat"]).dropna()
stops = gpd.GeoSeries(gpd.points_from_xy(stops["stop_lon"], stops["stop_lat"]), crs=4326).to_crs(utm)
# 30 segments per quarter circle, as sf's st_buffer()
area = boundary.make_valid().union_all().union(stops.union_all().convex_hull).buffer(3000, quad_segs=30)

folder = data_dir / "bho" / "network"
folder.mkdir(parents=True, exist_ok=True)
shutil.copyfile(feed, folder / "bhtrans.zip")
polygon = data_dir / "bho" / "cut.geojson"
gpd.GeoSeries([area], crs=utm).to_crs(4326).to_file(polygon)
pbf = folder / "bho.osm.pbf"
subprocess.run(["osmium", "extract", "--overwrite", "-p", str(polygon), str(sudeste),
                "-o", str(pbf)], check=True)
network = peabiru.build_network(folder)
print(f"{area.area / 1e6:.0f} km2, {pbf.stat().st_size / 1e6:.1f} MB")
print(network.info())

696 km2, 6.4 MB
{'vertices': 107414, 'edges': 286400, 'elevation': 'NONE', 'feeds': ['bhtrans'], 'stops': 9924, 'patterns': 1118, 'services': 14, 'frequencies': False}

Two checks before routing: build_network() refuses a feed with errors of high priority, and get_gtfs_errors() lists the others; check_transit_availability() says how much of the feed runs on the day chosen, Tuesday 17 November 2026.

print(len(peabiru.get_gtfs_errors(network)), "GTFS errors")
print(peabiru.check_transit_availability(network, dates=dt.date(2026, 11, 17)).to_string(index=False))

0 GTFS errors
      date  total_services  active_services  pct_active
2026-11-17              14                2    0.142857

Few services run because the calendar has one service per kind of day and of system, and only the weekday ones are due on a Tuesday.

docs.title: Residents, income and opportunities
docs.text:
Ipea's grid has, for each cell, the residents (P001), the average household income per person (R001), the income decile of the cell among the residents of the city (R003, 1 the poorest tenth), and the formal jobs (T001), public schools (E001) and public health facilities (S001). Each cell is routed from, and to, its centre.

grid = gpd.read_file(aop("hex_grid_bho.gpkg"))[["id_hex", "geometry"]]
people = pd.read_csv(aop("population_2010_bho.csv"))[["id_hex", "P001", "R001", "R003"]]
land = pd.read_csv(aop("landuse_2019_bho.csv"))[["id_hex", "T001", "E001", "S001"]]
cells = grid.merge(people, on="id_hex").merge(land, on="id_hex")
cells.columns = ["id", "geometry", "population", "income", "decile", "jobs", "schools", "health"]
centre = cells.geometry.to_crs(utm).centroid.to_crs(4326)
cells["lon"] = centre.x.round(6)
cells["lat"] = centre.y.round(6)
print(len(cells), "cells,", (cells["population"] > 0).sum(), "inhabited,",
      cells["population"].sum(), "residents,", cells["jobs"].sum(), "jobs,",
      cells["schools"].sum(), "schools,", cells["health"].sum(), "health facilities")

3049 cells, 2548 inhabited, 2409892 residents, 720512 jobs, 544 schools, 341 health facilities

docs.title: Access at the morning peak
docs.text:
For every inhabited cell, the jobs, schools and health facilities of the municipality reached within 30 and within 60 minutes, door to door, walking and riding, leaving at each minute from 07:00 to 07:59; the travel time to each destination is the median of those 60 departures.

table = pd.DataFrame(cells.drop(columns="geometry"))
origins = table[table["population"] > 0]
destinations = table[table["jobs"] + table["schools"] + table["health"] > 0]

    network, origins, destinations, opportunities_colnames=["jobs", "schools", "health"],
    mode=["WALK", "TRANSIT"], departure_datetime=dt.datetime(2026, 11, 17, 7, 0),
    time_window=60, percentiles=50, cutoffs=[30, 60], max_trip_duration=60, seed=42,
    progress=False,

      f"median {100 * share.to_numpy()[order][half]:.1f}% of the jobs within an hour")

mean 58.7%, median 71.2% of the jobs within an hour

docs.title: By income
docs.text:
The cells of each income decile, weighted by their residents: the mean share of the city's jobs within an hour, and of its public schools and health facilities within half an hour. The Palma ratio of access is the mean of the richest tenth over the mean of the poorest four tenths.

def by_decile(column):
    rows = access.dropna(subset="decile")
    share = rows[column] / table[column.split("_")[0]].sum()
    mean = lambda r: np.average(share[r.index], weights=r["population"])
    means = rows.groupby("decile").apply(mean, include_groups=False)
    palma = mean(rows[rows["decile"] == 10]) / mean(rows[rows["decile"] <= 4])
    means.index = means.index.astype(int)
    return pd.concat([(100 * means).round(1), pd.Series({"palma": round(palma, 2)})])

docs.title: Time against fare
docs.text:
A fare is a limit of its own: the fastest trip is of little use to someone who cannot pay for its transfers. peabiru routes with fares: a fare structure says what each ride costs and which transfers are discounted, max_fare keeps the fastest trip within a budget, and pareto_frontier() gives the travel time at each budget.

Belo Horizonte's feed has the fares by line, but its rules cannot be written faithfully as a fare structure (a transfer inside a MOVE station costs nothing, a second ride within 90 minutes costs half the cheaper fare); the R article has the details. So this part uses Porto Alegre: the sample data listed above (the centre and the neighbourhoods around it, as of May 2019) and its fare structure. The feeds only have service in the afternoon, so the departures are from 14:00 to 14:59 of Monday 13 May 2019.

poa_url = "https://raw.githubusercontent.com/ipea/r5r/v2.5.0/r-package/inst/extdata/poa/"
poa_dir = data_dir / "poa" / "network"
poa_dir.mkdir(parents=True, exist_ok=True)
for name in ["poa_osm.pbf", "poa_eptc.zip", "poa_trensurb.zip"]:
    fetch(poa_url + name, folder=poa_dir)
poa = peabiru.build_network(poa_dir)

print(fares["fares_per_transfer"].to_string(index=False))

The cells are the sample's grid (the same H3 cells as Ipea's), with the income quintile of each cell in the whole city (R002).

poa_cells = pd.read_csv(fetch(poa_url + "poa_hexgrid.csv", folder=poa_dir.parent))

docs.title: What a budget leaves
docs.text:
The jobs within an hour with at most one bus fare (R$ 4.80: a single ride), at most two (R$ 9.60: enough for either discounted transfer), and at any fare:

poa_departure = dt.datetime(2019, 5, 13, 14, 0)


def with_budget(max_fare):
    a = peabiru.accessibility(
        poa, poa_origins, poa_destinations, opportunities_colnames="jobs",
        mode=["WALK", "TRANSIT"], departure_datetime=poa_departure, time_window=60,
        percentiles=50, cutoffs=60, max_trip_duration=60, fare_structure=fares,
        max_fare=max_fare, draws_per_minute=1, progress=False,
    )
    return a.set_index("id")["accessibility"].reindex(poa_origins["id"]).to_numpy()


budget = poa_origins[["id", "population", "quintile"]].assign(
    one=with_budget(4.8), two=with_budget(9.6), any=with_budget(float("inf")))


def kept(rows):
    m = {b: np.average(rows[b], weights=rows["population"]) for b in ["one", "two", "any"]}
    return pd.Series({"jobs_any_fare": round(m["any"]),
                      "kept_one_fare": round(100 * m["one"] / m["any"], 1),
                      "kept_two_fares": round(100 * m["two"] / m["any"], 1)})


by_quintile = budget.groupby("quintile").apply(kept, include_groups=False)
by_quintile.index = [str(int(q)) for q in by_quintile.index]
by_quintile.loc["all"] = kept(budget)
print(by_quintile.to_string(float_format="{:g}".format))

pareto_frontier() gives, for a pair, the travel time at each fare cutoff where it changes: here the median over the departures of the hour, for three trips (the names of the neighbourhoods are OpenStreetMap's).

         ("89a9012830bffff", "89a901284c7ffff", "Petrópolis to Teresópolis")]
for origin, destination, trip in pairs:

        departure_datetime=poa_departure, time_window=60, fare_structure=fares,
        fare_cutoffs=[0, 4.5, 4.8, 7.2, 8.37, 9.6, 12], seed=42, progress=False,
    )

docs.title: Example: jobs by public transport in Helsinki
docs.text:
peabiru reads any OpenStreetMap extract and any valid GTFS feed; nothing in it is particular to Brazil. This example builds the network of the Helsinki capital region (Helsinki, Espoo, Vantaa and Kauniainen, 1.25 million residents on HSY's grid) from open data, and measures access to jobs by public transport at the morning peak.

The code blocks make one script; the output under each is what it prints, computed on 2026-11-12, and the numbers are those of the R example, which also explains why Helsinki was chosen among the candidate cities and why Lisbon was dropped. It downloads about 880 MB into PEABIRU_EXAMPLE_DATA and needs geopandas 1.0 or later and osmium.

Jobs within 45 minutes by public transport at the morning peak, computed below and drawn by site/figures/scenarios.R in the repository.

docs.text:
Data Source Licence Streets OpenStreetMap, extract of Finland by Geofabrik, dated 2026-11-11 (776 MB, MD5 ff7c5c52ce53880611989d15378b13af), cut with osmium to the box 24.45–25.30° E, 60.03–60.42° N ODbL 1.0 Public transport HSL (Helsinki Region Transport), GTFS feed https://infopalvelut.storage.hsldev.com/gtfs/hsl.zip, published 2026-11-12 05:42 (feed_version), valid 2026-11-11 to 2027-01-09, downloaded on 2026-11-12 (88 MB, SHA-256 1cd6f532…7223c); the feed is replaced every day CC BY 4.0 (HSL's open data terms); © HSL 2026 Residents HSY (Helsinki Region Environmental Services), Väestötietoruudukko 2025, residents on a 250 m grid (HSY's page of the dataset: updated 2026-07-08), from HSY's open WFS kartta.hsy.fi CC BY 4.0, © HSY Jobs HSY, Työpaikkaruudukko 2024, jobs (full-time equivalents) on a 250 m grid (updated 2026-08-26), same WFS CC BY 4.0, © HSY; original source: Statistics Finland's Business Register

Cells with fewer than five residents are left out of HSY's population grid, and one of its cells is not a place: HSY puts the residents it cannot assign to a building (33,575 in 2025, 2.6% of the total) in a cell in the sea, at the south-east corner of the grid; it is left out below. The job grid counts jobs in companies and non-profit organisations only, not public-sector jobs, as full-time equivalents, and gives -1 for cells with three or fewer employees, counted as 0 here: "jobs" below are a lower bound. It covers the wider Helsinki region (572,915 jobs); the box of this example keeps the 486,976 of the capital region, and leaves out the 42,516 without a location, which HSY puts in cells in the sea south of the box.

raw = root / "raw"
raw.mkdir(parents=True, exist_ok=True)
data_dir = root / "helsinki"


def fetch(url, name=None):

    if not dest.exists():
        part = dest.with_suffix(".part")
        urllib.request.urlretrieve(url, part)
        part.rename(dest)
    return dest

       "&typeNames=asuminen_ja_maankaytto:")

docs.title: The network
docs.text:
The streets: the capital region and a margin, cut from the extract of Finland. The timetables: HSL's feed holds two months of service (its stop_times.txt is 1.1 GB uncompressed), so it is cut to the trips that run on Tuesday 17 November 2026 and the rows of the other tables they use, copied unchanged; every stop is kept, and the tables peabiru does not read are left out (trips of Monday's service that run past midnight are not in the cut).

(data_dir / "network").mkdir(parents=True, exist_ok=True)
subprocess.run(["osmium", "extract", "--overwrite", "-s", "smart",
                "-b", "24.45,60.03,25.30,60.42", str(finland),
                "-o", str(data_dir / "network" / "helsinki.osm.pbf")], check=True)


def gtfs_one_day(src, date, out):
    """The trips of a GTFS feed that run on `date` (YYYYMMDD), and the rows of
    the other tables that belong to them, copied line by line."""
    z = zipfile.ZipFile(src)

    def table(name):
        return pd.read_csv(z.open(name), dtype=str, keep_default_na=False, encoding="utf-8-sig")

    day = dt.datetime.strptime(date, "%Y%m%d").strftime("%A").lower()
    cal = table("calendar.txt")
    active = set(cal.loc[(cal["start_date"] <= date) & (cal["end_date"] >= date) &
                         (cal[day] == "1"), "service_id"])
    cd = table("calendar_dates.txt")
    cd = cd[cd["date"] == date]
    active = (active - set(cd.loc[cd["exception_type"] == "2", "service_id"])) | \
        set(cd.loc[cd["exception_type"] == "1", "service_id"])
    trips = table("trips.txt")
    trips = trips[trips["service_id"].isin(active)]
    keep = {"trips.txt": ("trip_id", set(trips["trip_id"])),
            "stop_times.txt": ("trip_id", set(trips["trip_id"])),
            "routes.txt": ("route_id", set(trips["route_id"])),
            "shapes.txt": ("shape_id", set(trips["shape_id"])),
            "calendar.txt": ("service_id", active), "calendar_dates.txt": ("service_id", active)}
    tables = [t for t in ["agency.txt", "stops.txt", "routes.txt", "trips.txt",
                          "stop_times.txt", "calendar.txt", "calendar_dates.txt",
                          "frequencies.txt", "transfers.txt", "shapes.txt", "feed_info.txt",
                          "fare_attributes.txt", "fare_rules.txt"] if t in z.namelist()]
    with zipfile.ZipFile(out, "w", zipfile.ZIP_DEFLATED) as o:
        for name in tables:
            with z.open(name) as f, tempfile.TemporaryFile() as buf:
                lines = io.TextIOWrapper(f, encoding="utf-8", newline="")
                header = next(lines)
                buf.write(header.rstrip("\r\n").encode() + b"\n")
                col, ids = keep.get(name, (None, None))
                i = header.lstrip("﻿").rstrip("\r\n").split(",").index(col) if col else None
                for line in lines:
                    if i is None or next(csv.reader([line]))[i] in ids:
                        buf.write(line.rstrip("\r\n").encode() + b"\n")
                buf.seek(0)
                o.writestr(name, buf.read())
    return {"services": len(active), "trips": len(trips)}


print(gtfs_one_day(hsl, "20261117", data_dir / "network" / "hsl.zip"))

docs.title: Example: isochrones by mode
docs.text:
An isochrone is the area within a given travel time of a point. This example computes them for the four ways of travelling peabiru routes, from one park in Porto Alegre, and compares how far each mode gets in 10, 20 and 30 minutes. The code blocks make one script; the output shown under each is what it prints. It needs geopandas and, for the map, matplotlib.

The isochrones computed below. This figure is drawn from the same results, in the style of these pages, by site/figures/figures.R in the repository.

docs.title: The data
docs.text:
The example uses the sample data of Porto Alegre from the r5r project: an OpenStreetMap extract of the city, the GTFS feeds of its buses (EPTC) and of its metropolitan train (Trensurb), a hexagonal grid with population, jobs and schools, and a few points of interest. The files are downloaded once, into the temporary directory (about 2 MB):

import datetime as dt
import tempfile
import urllib.request
from pathlib import Path

import pandas as pd

import peabiru

poa = Path(tempfile.gettempdir()) / "peabiru-poa"
poa.mkdir(exist_ok=True)
url = "https://raw.githubusercontent.com/ipea/r5r/v2.5.0/r-package/inst/extdata/poa/"
for name in ["poa_osm.pbf", "poa_eptc.zip", "poa_trensurb.zip",
             "poa_hexgrid.csv", "poa_points_of_interest.csv"]:
    if not (poa / name).exists():
        urllib.request.urlretrieve(url + name, poa / name)

network = peabiru.build_network(poa)
print(network.info())

The bus feed of the sample only has trips between late morning and early evening on weekdays, so public transport is routed from 14:00 on a Monday:

poi = pd.read_csv(poa / "poa_points_of_interest.csv")
park = poi[poi["id"] == "farroupilha_park"]
print(park)
monday = dt.datetime(2019, 5, 13, 14, 0)

docs.title: Isochrones, mode by mode
docs.text:
isochrone() returns a GeoDataFrame with one polygon per origin and cutoff. The polygons are made from a grid of travel times; zoom sets how fine that grid is (from 9 to 12; at 11 a cell is about 65 m wide here). With public transport, the travel time of each cell is the median over the departures of time_window, here the 30 minutes from 14:00.

modes = {
    "Walking": "WALK",
    "Cycling": "BICYCLE",
    "Driving": "CAR",
    "Walking + public transport": ["WALK", "TRANSIT"],
}
parts = []
for label, mode in modes.items():
    iso = peabiru.isochrone(
        network, park, mode=mode, cutoffs=[10, 20, 30], zoom=11,
        departure_datetime=monday, time_window=30,
    )
    iso["mode"] = label
    parts.append(iso)
isochrones = pd.concat(parts, ignore_index=True)
print(isochrones.drop(columns=isochrones.geometry.name).head(4))

0  farroupilha_park       30.0        p50  Walking
1  farroupilha_park       20.0        p50  Walking
2  farroupilha_park       10.0        p50  Walking
3  farroupilha_park       30.0        p50  Cycling

The area of each isochrone, in square kilometres, sums up the picture (the polygons are projected to UTM zone 22S, EPSG:31982, to measure them):

isochrones["area_km2"] = isochrones.to_crs(31982).area.div(1e6).round(1)
print(isochrones.pivot(index="mode", columns="isochrone", values="area_km2")
      .loc[list(modes)])

mode                                          
Walking                      0.6    2.7    6.4
Cycling                      0.3    3.2   11.2
Driving                     15.1  102.8  142.6
Walking + public transport   0.6    4.5   20.3

Walking covers a couple of kilometres around the park in half an hour. Cycling covers no more than walking in the first ten minutes from this park, then pulls ahead. Driving reaches most of the extract within 20 minutes. Public transport sits in between, and its isochrones follow the bus corridors leaving the city centre: a stop within a short walk of the park and a fast ride extend the area far along those lines, and nowhere else.

With matplotlib, one panel per mode, the largest isochrone drawn first so that the shorter times stay on top:

for ax, (label, iso) in zip(axes.flat, isochrones.groupby("mode", sort=False)):
    for cutoff in (30, 20, 10):
        iso[iso["isochrone"] == cutoff].plot(ax=ax, color=colours[cutoff], alpha=0.8)
    ax.plot(park["lon"], park["lat"], "o", color="#1f2a2e", markeredgecolor="white")
