docs.title: Variations
docs.text:
• Several origins. Give isochrone() more than one point; the id column tells the polygons apart.
  • Streets instead of areas. polygon_output=False returns the street segments reached, each with its travel time, instead of polygons.
  • Traffic stress. Cycling uses the streets whose level of traffic stress is at most max_lts (2 by default) and walks the bike on the others. With max_lts=4, the 30-minute cycling isochrone from the park grows from 11.2 to 34.2 km².
  • Uncertainty. With percentiles=[25, 50, 75], public transport isochrones come in one set per percentile: the area reached on a lucky, a typical and an unlucky departure.

docs.title: Example: access to schools and health care in Recife and Caruaru
docs.text:
The other examples use small sample networks. This one starts from nothing, as a study of a real city would: it downloads the streets of two cities of Pernambuco, Brazil, from OpenStreetMap, places their residents on a grid with the census, takes the public schools and the primary health care units from the official registers, and measures how long it takes to reach the nearest of each, walking, cycling and driving.

  • Recife, the state capital (1.49 million people in the Censo 2022), on the coast, flat, crossed by rivers. Its street network is cut with 10 km around the municipality, which takes in the core of the metropolitan area (Olinda, Jaboatão dos Guararapes, Camaragibe and parts of Paulista and São Lourenço da Mata), so trips near the border can end in a neighbouring municipality.
  • Caruaru, 130 km inland in the Agreste (378 thousand people), a compact city in a large, mostly rural municipality, with 5 km around it.

The code blocks make one script, and every step works for any Brazilian municipality: change the IBGE code and the buffer. The output shown under each block is what it prints; it was computed on 2026-11-11. It needs geopandas 1.0 or later and, to cut the extract, osmium (brew install osmium-tool, apt install osmium-tool, or conda-forge).

Walking time to the nearest public school and primary health care unit, computed below. The figures of this page are drawn from the same results, in the style of these pages, by site/figures/pernambuco.R in the repository.

Streets only

No public, openly licensed GTFS feed was found for the buses of the Grande Recife Consórcio de Transporte or the metro (CBTU): it is not on the open-data portals of the city, the state or CBTU, nor in the Mobility Database. Caruaru has none either. So this example routes on the streets, and leaves public transport out rather than approximate it. With a GTFS feed, the same code takes mode=["WALK", "TRANSIT"] and a departure time: the Recife metropolitan region example does that, with the feed the consortium publishes on its own site (found after this page was written; it states no licence).

docs.title: The data
docs.text:
Data Source Licence Streets OpenStreetMap, extract of the Nordeste region by Geofabrik, dated 2026-11-01 (445 MB) ODbL 1.0 Municipal boundaries IBGE, malhas municipais (API, version 3) public data, IBGE Population IBGE, Censo Demográfico 2022, census tracts with their population, variable v0001 (44 MB for Pernambuco) public data, IBGE Schools INEP, Catálogo de Escolas 2023, with the coordinates of each school, as published by Ipea's geobr (schools_2023, 101 MB for Brazil) public data, INEP; geobr is MIT Health units CNES, Ministério da Saúde, through OpenDataSUS (cnes_estabelecimentos_csv.zip, 57 MB for Brazil, updated daily; downloaded on 2026-11-11) open data, Ministério da Saúde

The files are downloaded once into a directory of their own (set PEABIRU_EXAMPLE_DATA to keep it somewhere else):

import gzip
import os
import shutil
import subprocess
import urllib.request
import zipfile
from pathlib import Path

import geopandas as gpd
import numpy as np
import pandas as pd
from shapely.geometry import Polygon

import peabiru

data_dir = Path(os.environ.get("PEABIRU_EXAMPLE_DATA", "pe-data"))
raw = data_dir / "raw"
raw.mkdir(parents=True, exist_ok=True)


def fetch(url, name=None):
    dest = raw / (name or url.rsplit("/", 1)[1])
    if not dest.exists():
        part = dest.with_suffix(".part")
        with urllib.request.urlopen(url) as response, open(part, "wb") as out:
            # IBGE's API sends its answer gzip-compressed, asked or not
            gz = response.headers.get("Content-Encoding") == "gzip"
            shutil.copyfileobj(gzip.GzipFile(fileobj=response) if gz else response, out)
        part.rename(dest)
    return dest


nordeste = fetch("https://download.geofabrik.de/south-america/brazil/nordeste-261101.osm.pbf")
tracts_file = fetch("https://ftp.ibge.gov.br/Censos/Censo_Demografico_2022/"
                    "Agregados_por_Setores_Censitarios/malha_com_atributos/"
                    "setores/gpkg/UF/PE/PE_setores_CD2022.gpkg")
schools_file = fetch("https://www.ipea.gov.br/geobr/data_gpkg/schools/2023/schools_2023.gpkg")
cnes_file = fetch("https://s3.sa-east-1.amazonaws.com/ckan.saude.gov.br/CNES/"
                  "cnes_estabelecimentos_csv.zip")

cities = pd.DataFrame({"key": ["recife", "caruaru"],
                       "code": ["2611606", "2604106"],   # IBGE codes
                       "buffer": [10000, 5000]})         # metres
utm = 31985   # SIRGAS 2000 / UTM zone 25S, in metres, for both cities

docs.title: Streets: the municipality and a buffer
docs.text:
The boundary of each municipality comes from IBGE's API. Buffered in metres, it is the polygon osmium extract cuts the regional extract with; the cut goes in a directory of its own, which build_network() reads.

def boundary_of(code):
    url = ("https://servicodados.ibge.gov.br/api/v3/malhas/municipios/" + code +
           "?formato=application/vnd.geo+json&qualidade=maxima")
    b = gpd.read_file(fetch(url, f"{code}.geojson"))
    return b.to_crs(utm).make_valid()


def cut_streets(key, boundary, buffer):
    folder = data_dir / key / "network"
    folder.mkdir(parents=True, exist_ok=True)
    polygon = data_dir / key / "cut.geojson"
    # 30 segments per quarter circle, as sf's st_buffer()
    gpd.GeoSeries(boundary.buffer(buffer, quad_segs=30)).to_crs(4326).to_file(polygon)
    pbf = folder / f"{key}.osm.pbf"
    subprocess.run(["osmium", "extract", "--overwrite", "-p", str(polygon),
                    str(nordeste), "-o", str(pbf)], check=True)
    return folder


boundaries = {k: boundary_of(c) for k, c in zip(cities["key"], cities["code"])}
networks = {}
for k, b in zip(cities["key"], cities["buffer"]):
    folder = cut_streets(k, boundaries[k].geometry, b)
    networks[k] = peabiru.build_network(folder)
    print(k, f"{(folder / f'{k}.osm.pbf').stat().st_size / 1e6:.1f} MB", networks[k].info())

recife 16.0 MB {'vertices': 104331, 'edges': 275968, 'feeds': [], 'stops': 0, 'patterns': 0, 'services': 0, 'frequencies': False}
caruaru 1.9 MB {'vertices': 28445, 'edges': 78318, 'feeds': [], 'stops': 0, 'patterns': 0, 'services': 0, 'frequencies': False}

docs.title: Where people live: a hexagonal grid with the census
docs.text:
The census counts people by tract, and tracts vary from a city block to hundreds of square kilometres. A regular grid makes the cities comparable: hexagons 500 m apart, numbered row by row from the south-west, over the whole municipality. Each cell gets the population of the tracts it covers, in proportion to the area it covers of each.

def hex_grid(area, spacing=500):
    xmin, ymin, xmax, ymax = area.total_bounds
    h = spacing * np.sqrt(3) / 2
    r = spacing / np.sqrt(3)
    k = np.radians(30 + 60 * np.arange(7))   # pointy side up
    cells = []
    for j in range(-1, int(np.ceil((ymax - ymin) / h)) + 2):
        for i in range(-1, int(np.ceil((xmax - xmin) / spacing)) + 2):
            x = xmin + i * spacing + (j % 2) * spacing / 2
            y = ymin + j * h
            cells.append(Polygon(zip(x + r * np.cos(k), y + r * np.sin(k))))
    cells = gpd.GeoSeries(cells, crs=area.crs)
    cells = cells[cells.intersects(area.union_all())].reset_index(drop=True)
    return gpd.GeoDataFrame({"id": np.arange(1, len(cells) + 1)}, geometry=cells)


def population_grid(code, boundary):
    tracts = gpd.read_file(tracts_file, where=f"CD_MUN = '{code}'", columns=["v0001"])
    tracts = tracts.to_crs(utm)
    tracts["geometry"] = tracts.make_valid()
    tracts["tract_area"] = tracts.area
    cells = hex_grid(boundary)
    parts = gpd.overlay(cells, tracts, how="intersection", keep_geom_type=True)
    parts["people"] = parts["v0001"] * parts.area / parts["tract_area"]
    cells["population"] = cells["id"].map(parts.groupby("id")["people"].sum()).fillna(0)
    centres = cells.centroid.to_crs(4326)
    cells["lon"], cells["lat"] = centres.x.round(6), centres.y.round(6)
    cells["id"] = cells["id"].astype(str)
    return cells[cells["population"] > 0]


grids = {}
for k, code in zip(cities["key"], cities["code"]):
    grids[k] = population_grid(code, boundaries[k])
    print(f"{k:8} {len(grids[k]):5} cells, {grids[k]['population'].sum():,.0f} people")

recife    1107 cells, 1,488,797 people
caruaru   4489 cells, 378,048 people

The Censo 2022 counts 1,488,924 people in Recife and 378,048 in Caruaru; the grid keeps all but 127 in Recife, in tracts that reach slightly outside IBGE's municipal boundary. Caruaru's grid has four times as many cells as Recife's for a quarter of the people: most of the municipality is rural, and its large rural tracts spread a few people over each cell.

docs.title: Schools and health units
docs.text:
Schools: those of INEP's catalogue that are public (municipal, state or federal) and open with no restriction, and have coordinates. Health units: the CNES establishments of types 1 (posto de saúde) and 2 (centro de saúde / unidade básica), the primary health care units of the SUS, that are active and have coordinates. Both are taken over the whole area cut from OpenStreetMap, so the nearest unit can be across the municipal border, as it often is for people living near it.

def cut_area(key):
    return gpd.read_file(data_dir / key / "cut.geojson").to_crs(4674).union_all()


def schools_in(area):
    s = gpd.read_file(
        schools_file, bbox=area.bounds,
        columns=["code_school", "name_school", "name_muni"],
        where="admin_category = 'Pública' AND service_restriction = "
              "'ESCOLA EM FUNCIONAMENTO E SEM RESTRIÇÃO DE ATENDIMENTO'",
    )
    s = s[~s.geometry.is_empty & s.intersects(area)]
    return pd.DataFrame({"id": s["code_school"].astype(str), "name": s["name_school"],
                         "municipality": s["name_muni"],
                         "lon": s.geometry.x, "lat": s.geometry.y}).reset_index(drop=True)


with zipfile.ZipFile(cnes_file) as z, z.open("cnes_estabelecimentos.csv") as f:
    cnes = pd.read_csv(f, sep=";", encoding="latin1", dtype=str, keep_default_na=False,
                       usecols=["CO_CNES", "CO_UF", "CO_IBGE", "NO_FANTASIA", "TP_UNIDADE",
                                "CO_MOTIVO_DESAB", "NU_LATITUDE", "NU_LONGITUDE"])
cnes = cnes[(cnes["CO_UF"] == "26") & cnes["TP_UNIDADE"].isin(["1", "2"])
            & (cnes["CO_MOTIVO_DESAB"] == "") & (cnes["NU_LATITUDE"] != "")]


def health_in(area):
    h = pd.DataFrame({"id": cnes["CO_CNES"], "name": cnes["NO_FANTASIA"],
                      "municipality_code": cnes["CO_IBGE"],
                      "lon": cnes["NU_LONGITUDE"].astype(float),
                      "lat": cnes["NU_LATITUDE"].astype(float)})
    inside = gpd.GeoSeries(gpd.points_from_xy(h["lon"], h["lat"])).intersects(area).values
    return h[inside].reset_index(drop=True)


schools = {k: schools_in(cut_area(k)) for k in cities["key"]}
health = {k: health_in(cut_area(k)) for k in cities["key"]}
print(pd.DataFrame({k: {"schools": len(schools[k]), "health_units": len(health[k])}
                    for k in cities["key"]}))

              recife  caruaru
schools          937      216
health_units     511      102

A few things to know about these registers, seen while preparing them:

  • Of the public schools in operation, 22 of 486 in Recife and 15 of 168 in Caruaru have no coordinates in the catalogue and cannot be placed; they are left out.
  • Of the 167 active primary care units registered in Recife, six have coordinates outside the municipality: four a few hundred metres across the border, but one 24 km away, on the Ilha de Itamaracá, and one 20 km away, in Moreno. In Caruaru, two of 75 do, one of them 5 km out. Taking units by where they are rather than where they are registered keeps the far ones out of these figures (they fall outside the cut area), but those units are missing from their own neighbourhoods.
  • Schools and health units sit close to the streets of the extract: the median distance to the nearest street is 7 to 16 m, and a single school in each city is more than 300 m from one (418 m in Recife, 574 m in Caruaru), well within the 1.6 km at which peabiru links a point to the street network.

docs.title: Travel time to the nearest school and health unit
docs.text:
One travel-time matrix per city, mode and kind of unit, from every cell to every unit; the smallest time of each cell is its time to the nearest one. Driving is free flow (no congestion), and these networks are built without an elevation raster (a .tif raster in the data directory adds slope costs, see build_network()). The terrain example of the R site recomputes the shares below with slopes: on foot, within 15 minutes of a health unit, Recife goes from 75.8% to 73.7% and Caruaru from 68.0% to 65.8%, and within 30 minutes or by bicycle very little changes.

def nearest(k, mode, limit):
    out = grids[k][["id", "lon", "lat", "population"]].copy()
    for what, units in [("schools", schools[k]), ("health", health[k])]:
        m = peabiru.travel_time_matrix(networks[k], out, units, mode=mode,
                                       max_trip_duration=limit)
        out[what] = out["id"].map(m.groupby("from_id")["travel_time_p50"].min())
    return out                                  # NaN: none within the limit


def share_within(t, minutes):
    return [round(100 * t["population"][t[what] <= minutes].sum() / t["population"].sum(), 1)
            for what in ["schools", "health"]]


rows = []
for k in cities["key"]:
    for mode in ["WALK", "BICYCLE", "CAR"]:
        t = nearest(k, mode, limit=60)
        rows.append([k, mode, *share_within(t, 15), *share_within(t, 30)])
shares = pd.DataFrame(rows, columns=["city", "mode", "school_15", "health_15",
                                     "school_30", "health_30"])
print(shares)

      city     mode  school_15  health_15  school_30  health_30
0   recife     WALK       95.6       75.8       99.6       97.5
1   recife  BICYCLE       99.5       96.0       99.8       99.8
2   recife      CAR       99.2       99.2       99.2       99.2
3  caruaru     WALK       72.5       68.0       92.7       85.7
4  caruaru  BICYCLE       92.7       84.9       97.9       91.1
5  caruaru      CAR       99.8       98.2      100.0       99.9

The table is the share of the population (in %) within 15 and 30 minutes of the nearest public school and primary health care unit. In Recife, 96% of the people live within 15 minutes' walk of a public school and 76% of a health unit; in Caruaru, 73% and 68%. On a bicycle the gap narrows; by car, with free-flowing traffic, nearly everyone is within 15 minutes of both.

Recife's driving shares stop at 99.2% for a reason worth knowing: from 17 cells of Boa Viagem (about 12 thousand residents on this grid) there is no car route to the rest of the network on this extract, although the streets connect on foot and by bicycle. Removing every turn restriction from the extract does not reconnect them; the cause is in how the OpenStreetMap data of that area is read for cars, and is not identified yet. Checks like this one (cells or units that a mode never reaches) are worth running on any new extract.

docs.title: How many units within reach
docs.text:
The nearest unit is one measure; how many units are within reach is another, which accessibility() computes directly: here, the public schools within 15 minutes' walk of each cell, and the average over the population.

for k in cities["key"]:
    a = peabiru.accessibility(networks[k], grids[k][["id", "lon", "lat"]],
                              schools[k].assign(n=1), opportunities_colnames=["n"],
                              mode="WALK", cutoffs=15)
    people = a["id"].map(grids[k].set_index("id")["population"])
    print(k, round((a["accessibility"] * people).sum() / people.sum(), 1))

recife 4.6
caruaru 2.6

On average, a resident of Recife has between four and five public schools within a quarter of an hour on foot; one of Caruaru, between two and three.

docs.title: Isochrones from the centre
docs.text:
From Marco Zero, in Recife's old centre, and from the Feira de Caruaru, the area reached in 10, 20 and 30 minutes by each mode, in square kilometres:

centres = {
    "recife": pd.DataFrame({"id": ["Marco Zero"], "lon": [-34.8709722], "lat": [-8.063374]}),
    "caruaru": pd.DataFrame({"id": ["Feira de Caruaru"], "lon": [-35.9713866],
                             "lat": [-8.2897512]}),
}
rows = []
for k in cities["key"]:
    for mode in ["WALK", "BICYCLE", "CAR"]:
        iso = peabiru.isochrone(networks[k], centres[k], mode=mode,
                                cutoffs=[10, 20, 30], zoom=11)
        # the polygons come as traced, which can touch themselves: made valid
        # before measuring, as R's isochrone() returns them
        for minutes, km2 in zip(iso["isochrone"], iso.to_crs(utm).make_valid().area / 1e6):
            rows.append([k, mode, int(minutes), round(km2, 1)])
iso = pd.DataFrame(rows, columns=["city", "mode", "minutes", "km2"])
print(iso.pivot_table(index=["city", "mode"], columns="minutes", values="km2"))

minutes            10     20     30
city    mode                       
caruaru BICYCLE   1.2    8.9   23.4
        CAR      22.1  248.9  696.4
        WALK      0.1    1.5    4.7
recife  BICYCLE   0.8    3.0    8.2
        CAR       5.7  112.5  367.6
        WALK      0.4    1.3    3.0

One number here depends on more than routing: the 20-minute driving polygon of Caruaru has dozens of holes (pockets of the grid not reached in time) that touch each other. isochrone() returns the polygons as traced, and make_valid() (GEOS, in metres) repairs them keeping those holes: 248.9 km². The R package returns its polygons made valid with sf::st_make_valid() on longitude and latitude (s2), which merges many of the holes into the polygon: 285.9 km² in the R example. The other polygons agree to 0.1 km².

docs.text:
Each cell drawn as a dot at its centre, coloured by the walking time to the nearest health unit (needs matplotlib):

import matplotlib

import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

walk = nearest("recife", "WALK", limit=60)
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6, 7))
dots = ax.scatter(walk["lon"], walk["lat"], c=walk["health"].fillna(60), s=12,
                  cmap="OrRd_r", vmin=0, vmax=30)
ax.set_aspect(1 / np.cos(np.radians(8)))
ax.set_axis_off()

docs.title: Variations
docs.text:
• Another municipality. Change cities: the IBGE code (from https://servicodados.ibge.gov.br/api/v1/localidades/municipios), the buffer, the state of the census tracts (UF/PE/PE_setores_CD2022.gpkg) and of the CNES rows (CO_UF), and the Geofabrik region.
  • Large matrices on disk. With output_dir, travel_time_matrix() and accessibility() write one CSV file per origin instead of returning a data frame: the 4,489 × 216 driving matrix of Caruaru never has to fit in memory.
  • Gradual access. decay_function="logistic" (or "exponential", "linear") in accessibility() weighs each school by its distance in time instead of counting those under a hard limit.
  • Public transport. With a GTFS feed in the network directory, the same calls take mode=["WALK", "TRANSIT"], a departure_datetime and a time_window.
  • A browser map. The isochrone demo has the streets of Recife and of the urban area of Caruaru and draws isochrones wherever you click.

docs.title: Example: the Recife metropolitan region by public transport
docs.text:
The Região Metropolitana do Recife is 14 municipalities and 3.7 million people on the coast of Pernambuco, Brazil. Its buses, of ten operators under one authority, the Grande Recife Consórcio de Transporte Metropolitano, meet the metro and the VLT (light rail) of CBTU at integrated terminals, and the consortium publishes the timetables of all of them as one GTFS feed. This example builds the region as one network, from that feed and from OpenStreetMap, counts the public schools within reach of every resident on foot and by public transport, and draws isochrones by mode from the centre of Recife.

It is the Python half of a larger example: the R article also measures what the rail lines add, how much a trip varies with the minute one leaves, the options of one trip, and the speeds the timetable assumes. The numbers printed here are the ones of that article; they were computed on 2026-11-13. It needs geopandas 1.0 or later and, to cut the street extract, osmium.

From Praça do Derby by each mode, computed below; drawn by site/figures/rmr.R in the repository.

Data Source Licence Public transport Grande Recife Consórcio de Transporte Metropolitano, GTFS feed at https://www.granderecife.pe.gov.br/gtfs/gtfs.zip, feed_version v2026.10.26 (files of 2026-10-26; 38 MB): 395 bus routes of ten operators and, of CBTU's Metrorec, 3 metro and 2 VLT routes; timetables only published by the consortium at that address; no licence is stated in the feed Streets OpenStreetMap, extract of the Nordeste region by Geofabrik, dated 2026-11-01 (445 MB, MD5 93318fcddd85a53e8386eaa93588847c) ODbL 1.0 Municipal boundaries IBGE, malhas municipais (API, version 3) public data, IBGE Population IBGE, Censo Demográfico 2022, census tracts with their population, variable v0001 (44 MB for Pernambuco) public data, IBGE Schools INEP, Catálogo de Escolas 2023, with the coordinates of each school, as published by Ipea's geobr (schools_2023, 101 MB for Brazil) public data, INEP; geobr is MIT

The feed is not in the repository and is not redistributed: the code below uses a file granderecife-*.zip in the raw directory if there is one, or else downloads the consortium's current file. That address always serves the current version, so a later download is another network and gives other numbers; the checksum printed identifies the file used here.

No fares

The feed has a price for each route and no rule for transfers: the integration at the terminals, where passengers change lines without paying again, is not in it. A fare structure made from the feed would charge every boarding, so this example measures time and leaves money out.

import datetime as dt
import gzip
import hashlib
import os
import shutil
import subprocess
import urllib.request
import zipfile
from pathlib import Path

import geopandas as gpd
import numpy as np
import pandas as pd
import shapely
from shapely.geometry import Polygon

import peabiru

data_dir = Path(os.environ.get("PEABIRU_EXAMPLE_DATA", "rmr-data"))
raw = data_dir / "raw"
raw.mkdir(parents=True, exist_ok=True)


def fetch(url, name=None):
    dest = raw / (name or url.rsplit("/", 1)[1])
    if not dest.exists():
        part = dest.with_suffix(".part")
        request = urllib.request.Request(url, headers={"User-Agent": "peabiru-docs-examples"})
        with urllib.request.urlopen(request) as response, open(part, "wb") as out:
            # IBGE's API sends its answer gzip-compressed, asked or not
            gz = response.headers.get("Content-Encoding") == "gzip"
            shutil.copyfileobj(gzip.GzipFile(fileobj=response) if gz else response, out)
        part.rename(dest)
    return dest

docs.text:
The streets are cut from the regional extract with the 14 municipalities and 3 km around them. (Neighbouring boundaries do not share their vertices exactly: snapped to a grid of 1 cm, they join without slivers.) build_network() reads the directory with the cut and the feed.

utm = 31985   # SIRGAS 2000 / UTM zone 25S, in metres
threads = 4   # of this laptop's ten cores
# the municipalities of the region (IBGE codes): Recife, Olinda, Jaboatão dos
# Guararapes, Paulista, Camaragibe, São Lourenço da Mata, Cabo de Santo
# Agostinho, Ipojuca, Moreno, Igarassu, Abreu e Lima, Itapissuma, Ilha de
# Itamaracá and Araçoiaba
codes = ["2611606", "2609600", "2607901", "2610707", "2603454", "2613701", "2602902",
         "2607208", "2609402", "2606804", "2600054", "2607752", "2607604", "2601052"]

           "?formato=application/vnd.geo+json&qualidade=maxima")
    return gpd.read_file(fetch(url, f"{code}.geojson")).to_crs(utm).make_valid().union_all()


municipalities = gpd.GeoSeries([boundary_of(c) for c in codes], index=codes, crs=utm)
municipalities = gpd.GeoSeries(shapely.set_precision(municipalities.values, 0.01),

region = municipalities.union_all()

folder = data_dir / "rmr" / "network"

docs.title: Residents and schools
docs.text:
The census population goes on hexagonal cells 500 m apart, by the share of each tract's area that falls in each cell, and every cell is routed from its centre, as in the Recife and Caruaru example, which explains these steps. The schools are the public ones in operation in the area cut.

def hex_grid(area, spacing=500):
    xmin, ymin, xmax, ymax = area.bounds
    h = spacing * np.sqrt(3) / 2
    r = spacing / np.sqrt(3)
    k = np.radians(30 + 60 * np.arange(7))   # pointy side up
    cells = []
    for j in range(-1, int(np.ceil((ymax - ymin) / h)) + 2):
        for i in range(-1, int(np.ceil((xmax - xmin) / spacing)) + 2):
            x = xmin + i * spacing + (j % 2) * spacing / 2
            y = ymin + j * h
            cells.append(Polygon(zip(x + r * np.cos(k), y + r * np.sin(k))))
    cells = gpd.GeoSeries(cells, crs=utm)
    cells = cells[cells.intersects(area)].reset_index(drop=True)
    return gpd.GeoDataFrame({"id": np.arange(1, len(cells) + 1)}, geometry=cells)


tracts = gpd.read_file(tracts_file, columns=["v0001"],
                       where="CD_MUN IN (" + ", ".join(f"'{c}'" for c in codes) + ")").to_crs(utm)
tracts["geometry"] = tracts.make_valid()
tracts["tract_area"] = tracts.area
cells = hex_grid(region)
parts = gpd.overlay(cells, tracts, how="intersection", keep_geom_type=True)
parts["people"] = parts["v0001"] * parts.area / parts["tract_area"]
cells["population"] = cells["id"].map(parts.groupby("id")["people"].sum()).fillna(0)
centres = cells.centroid.to_crs(4326)
cells["lon"], cells["lat"] = centres.x.round(6), centres.y.round(6)
cells["id"] = cells["id"].astype(str)
cells = cells[cells["population"] > 0]

area = gpd.read_file(polygon).to_crs(4674).union_all()
s = gpd.read_file(
    schools_file, bbox=area.bounds, columns=["code_school", "name_school", "name_muni"],
    where="admin_category = 'Pública' AND service_restriction = "
          "'ESCOLA EM FUNCIONAMENTO E SEM RESTRIÇÃO DE ATENDIMENTO'")
s = s[~s.geometry.is_empty & s.intersects(area)]
schools = pd.DataFrame({"id": s["code_school"].astype(str), "lon": s.geometry.x,
                        "lat": s.geometry.y, "schools": 1}).reset_index(drop=True)
print(f"{len(cells):,} cells, {cells['population'].sum():,.0f} people, {len(schools):,} schools")

13,096 cells, 3,730,664 people, 1,203 schools

docs.text:
Cumulative access from every inhabited cell: the public schools reached within 30 and within 45 minutes, on foot and by public transport, and the average over the residents.

departure = dt.datetime(2026, 11, 10, 7, 0)
origins = cells[["id", "lon", "lat"]]
people = cells.set_index("id")["population"]

rows = {}
for name, mode in [("walk", "WALK"), ("transit", ["WALK", "TRANSIT"])]:
    a = peabiru.accessibility(network, origins, schools, opportunities_colnames="schools",
                              mode=mode, departure_datetime=departure, time_window=60,
                              percentiles=50, cutoffs=[30, 45], max_trip_duration=60,
                              n_threads=threads, progress=False)
    a["population"] = people.loc[a["id"]].to_numpy()
    rows[name] = {f"{cutoff:.0f} min": round(np.average(g["accessibility"], weights=g["population"]), 1)
                  for cutoff, g in a.groupby("cutoff")}

docs.title: Isochrones from the centre
docs.text:
From Praça do Derby, between the centre of Recife and its west and north: 74 of the feed's 400 routes stop within 400 m of the square on a weekday. isochrone() traces the areas on a grid of points, and the points just off the coast are reached from the seafront, so the polygons are cut at the coast (the municipal boundaries) before their area is measured. Walking is at 3.6 km/h and cycling at 12 km/h on streets of low traffic stress, the defaults; driving is at the speed limits, with no congestion.

derby = pd.DataFrame({"id": ["Praça do Derby"], "lon": [-34.8990], "lat": [-8.0570]})
rows = {}
for name, mode in [("walk", "WALK"), ("bicycle", "BICYCLE"), ("car", "CAR"),
                   ("transit", ["WALK", "TRANSIT"])]:
    iso = peabiru.isochrone(network, derby, mode=mode, cutoffs=[15, 30, 45], zoom=11,
                            departure_datetime=departure, time_window=60, n_threads=threads)
    # the polygons come as traced, which can touch themselves: made valid first
    on_land = iso.to_crs(utm).make_valid().intersection(region)
    rows[name] = {f"{minutes:.0f} min": round(km2, 1)
                  for minutes, km2 in zip(iso["isochrone"], on_land.area / 1e6)}
print(pd.DataFrame(rows).T)

         45 min  30 min  15 min
walk       15.2     6.6     1.5
bicycle    43.5    16.4     2.1
car      1453.0   618.4   105.9
transit   108.1    34.8     3.8

In 45 minutes public transport reaches 108 km² of land, cycling 44 and walking 15; a car in free-flowing traffic reaches 1,453 km², which no car does at 07:00.

docs.title: What is measured, and what is not
docs.text:
• Scheduled times, not observed ones. The timetable of the feed, as published. Its buses are scheduled slower at the peaks (15 km/h at 07:00 against 25 km/h at 04:00: the R article measures it), but delays, bunching, crowding and trips that do not run are not in it.
  • One day, one hour: departures from 07:00 to 07:59 on Tuesday 10 November 2026.
  • No fares: the feed has no rule for the integration at the terminals.
  • Rail included: the metro and the VLT are in the feed with their timetables. mode=["WALK", "BUS"] leaves them out.
  • Flat ground: no elevation raster. The terrain example shows how to add one.
  • Driving is free flow, an upper bound drawn for comparison.
  • Cells, not addresses: every trip starts at the centre of a cell 500 m from its neighbours; schools without coordinates in the catalogue are left out.

docs.title: Example: before and after in Porto Alegre
docs.text:
A transport plan is a list of changes: a cycle path here, a lane taken from cars there, a new clinic, a fare rule. Each one asks the same question twice, before and after. In peabiru the street network is built once, and the changes, called scenarios, are arguments of each routing call: new_lts changes the level of traffic stress cyclists meet on chosen streets, new_carspeeds and carspeed_scale change car speeds by street or by area, and a fare structure is a dictionary of tables that can be edited before the call. A new school or clinic is not even a change to the network: it is one more row among the destinations.

This example asks four such questions of Porto Alegre, on a small sample of the city, and times each one: a what-if is one routing call on the network as built, with nothing to edit and rebuild. The code blocks make one script; the output under each is what it prints, computed on 2026-11-12, and the numbers are those of the R example, whose figures are drawn from the same results by site/figures/scenarios.R in the repository. The fare routing takes a few minutes. It needs geopandas 1.0 or later.

Jobs gained by bicycle with a cycle path on Avenida Protásio Alves, computed below.

docs.title: The data
docs.text:
Data Source Licence Streets OpenStreetMap extract of Porto Alegre (poa_osm.pbf) ODbL 1.0, © OpenStreetMap contributors Public transport The EPTC bus and Trensurb train GTFS feeds (poa_eptc.zip, poa_trensurb.zip), cut for the sample: the buses run from 11:20 to 17:50 only, so the analyses below leave at 14:00 on Monday 13 May 2019 see below Grid poa_hexgrid.csv: 1,227 H3 cells (resolution 9) with population, jobs, schools and health facilities; its sources are not documented see below Fares fares/fares_poa.zip, the fare structure of the sample see below

All four are the sample data of Porto Alegre from the r5r project (its repository at the tag of version 2.5.0), whose licence line is GPL (>= 3) | MIT + file LICENSE. The sample also has an elevation raster, left out here: a call with a scenario routes without slope costs (with a warning), so the before and the after would not be comparable. The files are downloaded once into PEABIRU_EXAMPLE_DATA.

import copy
import datetime as dt
import os
import shutil
import time
import urllib.request
from pathlib import Path

import geopandas as gpd
import numpy as np
import pandas as pd
from shapely.geometry import Point

import peabiru

data_dir = Path(os.environ.get("PEABIRU_EXAMPLE_DATA", "example-data")) / "poa"
(data_dir / "network").mkdir(parents=True, exist_ok=True)
(data_dir / "fares").mkdir(exist_ok=True)
url = "https://raw.githubusercontent.com/ipea/r5r/v2.5.0/r-package/inst/extdata/poa/"
for f in ["poa_osm.pbf", "poa_eptc.zip", "poa_trensurb.zip", "poa_hexgrid.csv",
          "fares/fares_poa.zip"]:
    if not (data_dir / f).exists():
        urllib.request.urlretrieve(url + f, data_dir / f)
for f in ["poa_osm.pbf", "poa_eptc.zip", "poa_trensurb.zip"]:
    if not (data_dir / "network" / f).exists():
        shutil.copy(data_dir / f, data_dir / "network" / f)


def timed(f, *args, **kwargs):
    start = time.perf_counter()
    out = f(*args, **kwargs)
    return out, time.perf_counter() - start


threads = 4   # of this laptop's ten cores
network, build_time = timed(peabiru.build_network, data_dir / "network", n_threads=threads)
print(network.info())

grid = pd.read_csv(data_dir / "poa_hexgrid.csv")
grid[["jobs", "healthcare"]] = grid[["jobs", "healthcare"]].fillna(0)   # 5 cells have no count
print(grid[["population", "jobs", "schools", "healthcare"]].sum().astype(int).to_dict())

population = grid.set_index("id")["population"]


def per_resident(table, column="accessibility"):
    """The average of a column of a table with an id column over the residents."""
    w = population.loc[table["id"]].to_numpy()
    return float(np.average(table[column], weights=w))


osm = gpd.read_file(data_dir / "poa_osm.pbf", layer="lines")


def ways_named(name):
    return osm[(osm["name"] == name) & osm["highway"].notna()]

Building the network takes about a second; every call below is timed the same way, on a laptop with ten cores, four of them used, and other work running, so the timings are indications.

docs.title: A new cycle path
docs.text:
A cyclist who rides only on streets of low traffic stress (levels 1 and 2 of four, max_lts=2, the default) walks the bicycle on the others. In this extract Avenida Protásio Alves, the radial avenue east of the centre, is level 4 from end to end. What if it had a protected cycle path? The scenario gives its OpenStreetMap ways level 1:

ways = ways_named("Avenida Protásio Alves")
path = pd.DataFrame({"osm_id": ways["osm_id"].astype("int64"), "lts": 1})
print(len(path))


def jobs_by_bike(**scenario):
    return peabiru.accessibility(network, grid, grid, opportunities_colnames="jobs",
                                 mode="BICYCLE", max_lts=2, cutoffs=20, n_threads=threads,
                                 **scenario)


before, t_before = timed(jobs_by_bike)
after, t_after = timed(jobs_by_bike, new_lts=path)
gain = before[["id", "accessibility"]].merge(after[["id", "accessibility"]], on="id",
                                             suffixes=("_before", "_after"))
gainers = gain.loc[gain["accessibility_after"] > gain["accessibility_before"], "id"]
print(round(per_resident(gain, "accessibility_before")),
      round(per_resident(gain, "accessibility_after")),
      round(population.loc[gainers].sum() / population.sum(), 3))

94
30069 31075 0.312

One ride across it, from the east end of the avenue to the Santa Casa hospital in the centre, before and after:

ends = pd.DataFrame({"id": ["Jardim Carvalho", "Santa Casa"],
                     "lon": [-51.1405, -51.2224], "lat": [-30.0415, -30.03043]})
monday = dt.datetime(2019, 5, 13, 14, 0)


def ride(**scenario):
    return peabiru.detailed_itineraries(network, ends.iloc[[0]], ends.iloc[[1]],
                                        mode="BICYCLE", max_lts=2,
                                        departure_datetime=monday, **scenario)


for when, r in [("today", ride()), ("with the path", ride(new_lts=path))]:

docs.title: Congestion and a closed avenue
docs.text:
peabiru's car speeds are free flow: the speed limit of each street, or a default by its class, with no traffic. Two scenarios change that: every street within 2 km of the Mercado Público at half its speed, and Avenida Ipiranga, the east–west arterial along the Dilúvio creek, closed to cars.

# 16 segments per quarter circle, as st_buffer(nQuadSegs = 16) in the R example
centre = gpd.GeoSeries([Point(-51.22781, -30.02756)], crs=4326).to_crs(31982)
slow_centre = gpd.GeoDataFrame({"poly_id": ["centre"], "scale": [0.5], "priority": [1]},
                               geometry=centre.buffer(2000, quad_segs=16).to_crs(4326))
ipiranga = ways_named("Avenida Ipiranga")
closed = pd.DataFrame({"osm_id": ipiranga["osm_id"].astype("int64"), "max_speed": 0.0,
                       "speed_type": "km/h"})


def drive(**scenario):
    m = peabiru.travel_time_matrix(network, grid, grid, mode="CAR", n_threads=threads,
                                   **scenario)
    return m[["from_id", "to_id", "travel_time_p50"]]


base, t_base = timed(drive)
slow, t_slow = timed(drive, new_carspeeds=slow_centre)
shut, t_shut = timed(drive, new_carspeeds=closed)


def change(scenario):
    m = base.merge(scenario, on=["from_id", "to_id"], how="left", suffixes=("", "_s"))
    after = m["travel_time_p50_s"].astype("float").fillna(120)   # no longer within the limit
    d = after - m["travel_time_p50"].astype("float")
    return float(round(d.mean(), 3)), float(round((d > 0).mean(), 3)), float(d.max())


print(len(base), change(slow), change(shut))

1483605 (0.348, 0.143, 9.0) (0.73, 0.137, 119.0)

Over all 1,483,605 pairs of cells, the slower centre adds 0.35 minutes on average and the closed avenue 0.73 (each scenario slows 14% of the pairs; a pair no longer reached within the two-hour limit counts as 120 minutes): small numbers, because most pairs do not cross either.

Access to health facilities by car, within 10 minutes, on average over the residents:

def health_by_car(**scenario):
    a = peabiru.accessibility(network, grid, grid, opportunities_colnames="healthcare",
                              mode="CAR", cutoffs=10, n_threads=threads, **scenario)
    return round(per_resident(a), 2)


print(health_by_car(), health_by_car(new_carspeeds=slow_centre),
      health_by_car(new_carspeeds=closed))

35.51 32.35 33.43

And access to public transport by car: with mode=["CAR", "TRANSIT"] a trip may drive to any stop and board there, or drive all the way. In this sample the direct drive is always faster, before and after:

def legs(**scenario):

docs.title: Example: terrain, in Salvador (Bahia) and Olinda (Pernambuco)
docs.text:
What do slopes change in walking and cycling times? This example builds two cities built on hills, Salvador (Bahia, 2.4 million people in the Censo 2022, a city split by an escarpment between its upper and lower towns) and Olinda (Pernambuco, 350 thousand, a historic centre on hills next to a flat coastal strip), each twice: on flat ground, and with an elevation raster from the Copernicus DEM (GLO-90, 3 arc seconds), with Tobler's hiking function and with Minetti's energy cost. Then it measures the areas reached from the centre and the time from every resident to the nearest public school and primary health care unit.

The code blocks make one script; the output shown under each block is what it prints, computed on 2026-11-12. It repeats, step by step, the cities of hills of the R example, and prints the same numbers; the R example also covers the Recife metropolitan region and five more municipalities of Pernambuco, and compares GLO-90 with GLO-30 (see Which raster below). It needs geopandas 1.0 or later and two command-line tools: osmium to cut the street extract and GDAL's gdalwarp to cut the elevation model (brew install osmium-tool gdal, apt install osmium-tool gdal-bin, or conda-forge).

From the Praça Municipal, on foot and by bicycle, flat and with slopes, computed below; drawn by site/figures/terrain.R in the repository.

Streets only

No open GTFS feed was found for Salvador, and neither Bahia nor Pernambuco has one in the Mobility Database. So this example routes on the streets. (Grande Recife publishes a feed on its own site, found after this page was written: the Recife metropolitan region example routes on it.)

import gzip
import math
import os

import urllib.request

from pathlib import Path

import numpy as np
import pandas as pd
from shapely.geometry import Polygon

import peabiru

data_dir = Path(os.environ.get("PEABIRU_EXAMPLE_DATA", "terrain-data"))
raw = data_dir / "raw"
raw.mkdir(parents=True, exist_ok=True)


def fetch(url, name=None):
    dest = raw / (name or url.rsplit("/", 1)[1])
    if not dest.exists():
        part = dest.with_suffix(".part")
        with urllib.request.urlopen(url) as response, open(part, "wb") as out:
            # IBGE's API sends its answer gzip-compressed, asked or not
            gz = response.headers.get("Content-Encoding") == "gzip"
            shutil.copyfileobj(gzip.GzipFile(fileobj=response) if gz else response, out)
        part.rename(dest)
    return dest

cities = pd.DataFrame({

docs.title: Streets and elevation
docs.text:
The streets are cut from the regional extract with the municipality and 3 km around it, as in the Recife and Caruaru example. The elevation model is cut over the box of those streets: GDAL reads only the parts of the Copernicus tiles it needs, straight from the AWS registry, and the crop keeps the tiles' own grid (no resampling). The sea has no tiles; the documentation of the registry says to take it as 0 m, which INIT_DEST=0 does. The extract goes in two directories: network/ alone, and network-dem/ with the raster, which turns slope costs on.

dem_url = ("https://copernicus-dem-90m.s3.amazonaws.com/Copernicus_DSM_COG_30_{0}_00_{1}_00_DEM/"
           "Copernicus_DSM_COG_30_{0}_00_{1}_00_DEM.tif")


def boundary_of(code, utm):
    url = ("https://servicodados.ibge.gov.br/api/v3/malhas/municipios/" + code +
           "?formato=application/vnd.geo+json&qualidade=maxima")
    b = gpd.read_file(fetch(url, f"{code}.geojson"))
    return b.to_crs(utm).make_valid()


def cut_streets(key, boundary, buffer):
    folder = data_dir / key / "network"
    folder.mkdir(parents=True, exist_ok=True)
    polygon = data_dir / key / "cut.geojson"
    # 30 segments per quarter circle, as sf's st_buffer()
    gpd.GeoSeries(boundary.buffer(buffer, quad_segs=30)).to_crs(4326).to_file(polygon)
    pbf = folder / f"{key}.osm.pbf"
    subprocess.run(["osmium", "extract", "--overwrite", "-p", str(polygon),
                    str(nordeste), "-o", str(pbf)], check=True)
    return pbf


def exists(url):
    try:
        with urllib.request.urlopen(urllib.request.Request(url, method="HEAD")):
            return True
    except OSError:
        return False


def cut_dem(key, pbf):
    folder = data_dir / key / "network-dem"
    folder.mkdir(exist_ok=True)
    if not (folder / pbf.name).exists():
        os.link(pbf, folder / pbf.name)
    # the box of the extract's streets, not of the cut: osmium keeps whole the
    # ways that cross the cut, and peabiru takes points off the raster as 0 m
    streets = folder / "streets.osm.pbf"
    subprocess.run(["osmium", "tags-filter", "--overwrite", str(pbf), "w/highway",
                    "-o", str(streets)], check=True)
    box = subprocess.run(["osmium", "fileinfo", "-e", "-g", "data.bbox", str(streets)],
                         check=True, capture_output=True, text=True).stdout
    streets.unlink()
    xmin, ymin, xmax, ymax = (float(v) for v in box.strip("()\n").split(","))
    px = 3 / 3600   # pixels centred on the 3-arc-second grid: edges half a pixel off
    te = [(math.floor(xmin / px - 0.5) + 0.5) * px, (math.floor(ymin / px - 0.5) + 0.5) * px,
          (math.ceil(xmax / px - 0.5) + 0.5) * px, (math.ceil(ymax / px - 0.5) + 0.5) * px]
    tiles = []
    for lat in range(math.floor(te[1]), math.floor(te[3]) + 1):
        for lon in range(math.floor(te[0]), math.floor(te[2]) + 1):
            ns = f"{'S' if lat < 0 else 'N'}{abs(lat):02d}"
            ew = f"{'W' if lon < 0 else 'E'}{abs(lon):03d}"
            if exists(dem_url.format(ns, ew)):
                tiles.append("/vsicurl/" + dem_url.format(ns, ew))
    tif = folder / f"{key}_dem.tif"
    subprocess.run(["gdalwarp", "-q", "-overwrite", "-of", "GTiff", *tiles, str(tif),
                    "-te", *[f"{v:.10f}" for v in te], "-tr", f"{px:.15f}", f"{px:.15f}",
                    "-r", "near", "-wo", "INIT_DEST=0", "-ot", "Float32",
                    "-co", "COMPRESS=DEFLATE", "-co", "PREDICTOR=3", "-co", "TILED=YES"],
                   check=True)
    return len(tiles), tif


boundaries = {}
for key, c in cities.iterrows():
    boundaries[key] = boundary_of(c["code"], c["utm"])
    pbf = cut_streets(key, boundaries[key].geometry, c["buffer"])
    n, tif = cut_dem(key, pbf)
    print(f"{key:8} streets {pbf.stat().st_size / 1e6:5.1f} MB, "
          f"elevation {n} tiles, {tif.stat().st_size / 1e6:4.1f} MB")

docs.title: Which raster
docs.text: The Copernicus DEM is a surface model: it measures the top of whatever the radar saw, buildings and trees included. At 1 arc second (GLO-30, the same address with 30m and COG_10) a street between towers reads metres above its neighbour, and since peabiru samples the raster every 10 m along each street, at the nearest pixel, those steps become slopes. The R example measures it on a flat district of towers in Recife, where slopes should cost nothing: GLO-30 adds a minute to the average walk to a health unit, GLO-90 0.15 of a minute. So this example uses GLO-90, which averages the roofs away, and with them the short steep streets: its slope costs are on the low side. A terrain model (bare earth) at a finer resolution, where one exists, is the better input.

docs.title: Where people live, and the units
docs.text:
A hexagonal grid with the population of the census tracts (500 m apart in Salvador, 250 m in the small municipality of Olinda), public schools from INEP and primary health care units from CNES, over the cut area, as in the Recife and Caruaru example.

def hex_grid(area, spacing):
    xmin, ymin, xmax, ymax = area.total_bounds
    h = spacing * np.sqrt(3) / 2
    r = spacing / np.sqrt(3)
    k = np.radians(30 + 60 * np.arange(7))   # pointy side up
    cells = []
    for j in range(-1, int(np.ceil((ymax - ymin) / h)) + 2):
        for i in range(-1, int(np.ceil((xmax - xmin) / spacing)) + 2):
            x = xmin + i * spacing + (j % 2) * spacing / 2
            y = ymin + j * h
            cells.append(Polygon(zip(x + r * np.cos(k), y + r * np.sin(k))))
    cells = gpd.GeoSeries(cells, crs=area.crs)
    cells = cells[cells.intersects(area.union_all())].reset_index(drop=True)
    return gpd.GeoDataFrame({"id": np.arange(1, len(cells) + 1)}, geometry=cells)


def population_grid(c, boundary):
    tracts = gpd.read_file(tracts_file[c["uf"]], where=f"CD_MUN = '{c['code']}'",
                           columns=["v0001"])
    tracts = tracts.to_crs(c["utm"])
    tracts["geometry"] = tracts.make_valid()
    tracts["tract_area"] = tracts.area
    cells = hex_grid(boundary, c["spacing"])
    parts = gpd.overlay(cells, tracts, how="intersection", keep_geom_type=True)
    parts["people"] = parts["v0001"] * parts.area / parts["tract_area"]
    cells["population"] = cells["id"].map(parts.groupby("id")["people"].sum()).fillna(0)
    centres = cells.centroid.to_crs(4326)
    cells["lon"], cells["lat"] = centres.x.round(6), centres.y.round(6)
    cells["id"] = cells["id"].astype(str)
    return cells[cells["population"] > 0]


def schools_in(area):
    s = gpd.read_file(
        schools_file, bbox=area.bounds,
        columns=["code_school", "name_school", "name_muni"],
        where="admin_category = 'Pública' AND service_restriction = "
              "'ESCOLA EM FUNCIONAMENTO E SEM RESTRIÇÃO DE ATENDIMENTO'",
    )
    s = s[~s.geometry.is_empty & s.intersects(area)]
    return pd.DataFrame({"id": s["code_school"].astype(str), "lon": s.geometry.x,
                         "lat": s.geometry.y}).reset_index(drop=True)


with zipfile.ZipFile(cnes_file) as z, z.open("cnes_estabelecimentos.csv") as f:
    cnes = pd.read_csv(f, sep=";", encoding="cp1252", dtype=str, keep_default_na=False,
                       usecols=["CO_CNES", "CO_UF", "TP_UNIDADE", "CO_MOTIVO_DESAB",
                                "NU_LATITUDE", "NU_LONGITUDE"])
cnes = cnes[cnes["TP_UNIDADE"].isin(["1", "2"]) & (cnes["CO_MOTIVO_DESAB"] == "")
            & (cnes["NU_LATITUDE"] != "") & (cnes["NU_LONGITUDE"] != "")]


def health_in(area, uf_code):
    h = cnes[cnes["CO_UF"] == uf_code]
    h = pd.DataFrame({"id": h["CO_CNES"], "lon": h["NU_LONGITUDE"].astype(float),
                      "lat": h["NU_LATITUDE"].astype(float)})
    inside = gpd.GeoSeries(gpd.points_from_xy(h["lon"], h["lat"])).intersects(area).values
    return h[inside].reset_index(drop=True)


grids, schools, health = {}, {}, {}
for key, c in cities.iterrows():
    area = gpd.read_file(data_dir / key / "cut.geojson").to_crs(4674).union_all()
    grids[key] = population_grid(c, boundaries[key])
    schools[key] = schools_in(area)
    health[key] = health_in(area, c["uf_code"])
    print(f"{key:8} {len(grids[key]):5} cells, {grids[key]['population'].sum():,.0f} people, "
          f"{len(schools[key])} schools, {len(health[key])} health units")

docs.text:
def nearest(key, model, mode, max_lts=2):
    out = grids[key][["id", "lon", "lat", "population"]].copy()
    for what, units in [("schools", schools[key]), ("health", health[key])]:
        m = peabiru.travel_time_matrix(networks[key, model], out, units, mode=mode,
                                       max_lts=max_lts, max_trip_duration=60)
        out[what] = out["id"].map(m.groupby("from_id")["travel_time_p50"].min())
    return out                                  # NaN: none within the hour


def share(t, what, minutes=15):
    return round(100 * t["population"][t[what] <= minutes].sum() / t["population"].sum(), 1)


def mean_minutes(t, what="health"):
    ok = t[what].notna()
    return round(np.average(t[what][ok], weights=t["population"][ok]), 2)


rows = []
for key in cities.index:
    for mode in ["WALK", "BICYCLE"]:

docs.title: Example: how much a trip by public transport varies
docs.text: By car or on foot, a trip takes the same time whenever it starts. By public transport it does not: it depends on when the next vehicle leaves. This example measures that variation in two ways, with percentiles over a window of departures, and trip by trip. The code blocks make one script; the output shown under each is what it prints.

docs.title: Percentiles on a frequency-based network
docs.text:
The São Paulo sample that ships with the package has a feed described by frequencies ("a bus every 8 minutes") rather than timetables. For such routes peabiru draws random schedules consistent with the frequencies, 5 per departure minute by default, so the travel times of a window of departures form a distribution. seed makes the draws reproducible.

points = peabiru.sample_points()
monday = dt.datetime(2019, 5, 13, 14, 0)

    network, points.iloc[:1], points.iloc[1:],
    mode=["WALK", "TRANSIT"],
    departure_datetime=monday,
    time_window=60,
    percentiles=[5, 25, 50, 75, 95],
    seed=42,
)
ttm = ttm.sort_values(["travel_time_p50", "travel_time_p95"], ignore_index=True)
print(ttm.drop(columns="from_id").iloc[::5].to_string())

docs.title: Facility location
docs.text: Travel times say how well a place is served today. locate_facilities() turns the question around: given the people to serve and the places where a facility could open, where should the next ones go? floating_catchment() measures the other side of access, supply against the demand that competes for it. Both work on the travel times of the network, by any mode, and both are peabiru's own functions.

docs.title: The four models
docs.text:
locate_facilities() takes the demand points (with a weight each: residents, pupils, patients), the candidate sites and, optionally, the facilities that already exist, and solves one of four classic models:

model question objective "max_cover" with n_facilities new facilities, how many people can be within cutoff minutes of one? demand covered (to maximise) "set_cover" how few facilities put everyone within cutoff minutes? number of new sites "p_median" where do n_facilities facilities make the average trip shortest? demand-weighted minutes to the nearest facility "p_center" where do they make the worst trip shortest? minutes of the demand point farthest from its nearest facility

A demand point is covered by a site at most cutoff minutes away (the cutoff included). The existing facilities count first: only the demand they leave uncovered, or the travel time they leave, drives the choice of the new sites, and they are never closed or moved.

docs.title: A worked example: two new schools
docs.text:
The sample network has 27 points with their population; six of them have a school. Where would two more schools put the most residents within a 12-minute walk of one?

import peabiru

network = peabiru.build_network(peabiru.sample_data_path(), n_threads=2)
points = peabiru.sample_points()
schools = points[points["schools"] > 0]
others = points[points["schools"] == 0]

found = peabiru.locate_facilities(
    network, points, others, existing=schools,
    model="max_cover", n_facilities=2, cutoff=12,
    demand_colname="population", mode="WALK", n_threads=2,
)
print(found.sites[["id", "order", "marginal", "cumulative"]].to_string(index=False))

      f"({100 * s['covered_before'] / s['total_demand']:.1f}%)")
print(f"greedy:         {s['objective_greedy']:.0f}")
print(f"after {s['n_swaps']} swap:   {s['covered']:.0f} "
      f"({100 * s['covered'] / s['total_demand']:.1f}%)")

docs.title: How the models are solved
docs.text:
By heuristics, with no integer programming solver:

  1. Greedy construction. Sites are opened one at a time, each the one that improves the objective most given the ones already open. For maximal covering this covers at least 63% (1 - 1/e) of the most that any choice of n_facilities sites could cover of the demand not covered today (Nemhauser, Wolsey and Fisher, 1978); in practice it is usually much closer.
  2. Vertex substitution (swap=True, the default; Teitz and Bart, 1968). An open new site is swapped for a closed candidate while that improves the objective, taking the best swap of all at each step. The result is never worse than the greedy one, and summary reports both (objective_greedy, objective, n_swaps).

In the example the greedy pair covers 46,040 residents and one swap takes it to 46,217, which is the optimum: an exhaustive search over the 210 pairs of candidates finds nothing better. That is not guaranteed in general; the solutions are good and reproducible, not proven optimal.

Details by model:

  • "set_cover" opens the site that covers the most demand points not yet covered until every point some site can cover is covered, then drops the sites the others make redundant.
  • "p_center" compares the largest travel time and, on ties, the demand-weighted sum, in the greedy step and in the swaps.
  • In "set_cover" and "p_center" a point with weight 0 is not demand, and the others count the same whatever their weight.
  • In "p_median" and "p_center", a demand point that reaches no open facility within max_trip_duration is charged unreachable_time minutes (by default twice the longest travel time of the table), so that serving a point always beats shortening the trip of another. A point that no site at all can serve is left out of the objective and reported in summary["unservable_demand"].
  • Ties go to the candidate listed first, and the result does not depend on n_threads.

    demand_colname="population", mode="WALK", n_threads=2,

print(len(cover.sites), "sites;", cover.summary["unservable_demand"], "residents out of reach")

for model in ("p_median", "p_center"):

        network, points, points, model=model, n_facilities=2,
        demand_colname="population", mode="WALK", max_trip_duration=60, n_threads=2,

docs.title: Supply against demand: the floating catchment area
docs.text:
Being near a school is not the same as having a place in it. floating_catchment() computes the two-step floating catchment area (Luo and Wang, 2003):

  1. each facility's supply is divided by the demand within its catchment;
  2. each demand point adds up the ratios of the facilities within its catchment.

The result is supply per unit of demand at each demand point: here, schools per resident within a 20-minute walk.

fca = peabiru.floating_catchment(
    network, points, schools, cutoff=20,
    demand_colname="population", supply_colname="schools", mode="WALK", n_threads=2,
)
print(fca.supply[["id", "supply", "catchment_demand"]].to_string(index=False))
per_10k = 10_000 * fca.demand["accessibility"]
print(f"schools per 10,000 residents: from {per_10k.min():.2f} to {per_10k.max():.2f}")
print(f"shared out: {(fca.demand['demand'] * fca.demand['accessibility']).sum():.1f} schools")

89a8100c1dbffff     2.0           17501.0
89a8100c39bffff     1.0           10593.0
89a8100c1cbffff     1.0           21263.0

The index shares out the supply: the sum over the demand points of demand times accessibility is the supply of the facilities that have any demand in their catchment.

With decay_function="step" a pair counts in full up to cutoff minutes and not at all beyond. Any other decay function gives the enhanced form (Luo and Qi, 2009), in which nearer pairs weigh more, in both steps. The functions and their decay_value are those of accessibility(); the weight falls continuously with travel time, where Luo and Qi used a few travel-time zones.

smooth = peabiru.floating_catchment(
    network, points, schools, cutoff=20, decay_function="logistic", decay_value=5,
    demand_colname="population", supply_colname="schools", mode="WALK", n_threads=2,
)
per_10k = 10_000 * smooth.demand["accessibility"]
print(f"schools per 10,000 residents: from {per_10k.min():.2f} to {per_10k.max():.2f}")

docs.title: From a table of travel times
docs.text:
Both functions take a table of travel times instead of a network: from_id (demand point), to_id (site) and the minutes in travel_time_pXX or travel_time, as travel_time_matrix() returns it. A pair that is absent is unreachable. The points then need only their id, so the same matrix can serve several models, or travel times from another source can be used.

import pandas as pd

sites = pd.concat([schools, others])
times = peabiru.travel_time_matrix(
    network, points, sites, mode="WALK", max_trip_duration=12, n_threads=2,
)
again = peabiru.locate_facilities(
    None, points[["id", "population"]], others[["id"]], existing=schools[["id"]],
    model="max_cover", n_facilities=2, cutoff=12, demand_colname="population",
    travel_times=times,
)
print(list(again.sites["id"]) == list(found.sites["id"]))

True

docs.title: What the models do not see
docs.text: The models choose sites by travel time and demand alone. They do not know the capacity or the cost of a facility, whether land is available at a candidate site, the demand that comes from outside the study area, or how well the people already covered are served. Maximal covering treats 11 minutes and 1 minute alike, and p-median may leave a few people very far to shorten the average: comparing two models on the same data is often more informative than either alone.

docs.title: Fares
docs.text:
peabiru computes transit fares from a fare structure, which describes how much each ride costs and which transfers are discounted, and the routing functions take it as fare_structure. With one, public transport is routed with the multi-criteria router (McRAPTOR), which keeps at each stop the trips that are faster or cheaper than the others.

The examples use the sample data of Porto Alegre from the r5r project, with its fare structure, downloaded once into the temporary directory (about 2 MB); its GTFS feeds only have service in the afternoon, hence the 14:00 departure.

import datetime as dt
import tempfile
import urllib.request
from pathlib import Path

import pandas as pd

import peabiru

poa = Path(tempfile.gettempdir()) / "peabiru-poa"
poa.mkdir(exist_ok=True)
url = "https://raw.githubusercontent.com/ipea/r5r/v2.5.0/r-package/inst/extdata/poa/"
for name in ["poa_osm.pbf", "poa_eptc.zip", "poa_trensurb.zip", "poa_hexgrid.csv"]:
    if not (poa / name).exists():
        urllib.request.urlretrieve(url + name, poa / name)
fares_zip = Path(tempfile.gettempdir()) / "peabiru-fares_poa.zip"
if not fares_zip.exists():
    urllib.request.urlretrieve(url + "fares/fares_poa.zip", fares_zip)

network = peabiru.build_network(poa)
points = pd.read_csv(poa / "poa_hexgrid.csv")
departure = dt.datetime(2019, 5, 13, 14, 0)

docs.title: The fare structure
docs.text:
setup_fare_structure() builds one where every route, fare type and transfer costs the same; edit it to follow the fare rules of the city. read_fare_structure() reads one written by write_fare_structure(), here or in the R package.

fares = peabiru.read_fare_structure(fares_zip)
print(fares["fares_per_type"])
print(fares["fares_per_transfer"])
print(fares["max_discounted_transfers"], fares["transfer_time_allowance"], fares["fare_cap"])

   type  unlimited_transfers  allow_same_route_transfer  use_route_fare  fare
0   BUS                False                      False           False   4.8
1  RAIL                 True                      False           False   4.5
  first_leg second_leg  fare
0       BUS        BUS  7.20
1      RAIL        BUS  8.37
2       BUS       RAIL  8.37
1 60 inf

A bus ride costs 4.80 and a train ride 4.50; two buses within 60 minutes cost 7.20 together, a bus and a train 8.37; one discounted transfer per trip; the trains have unlimited transfers between them. Every GTFS route gets its fare type in fares_per_route (matched by agency_id and route_id); a route missing from it is an error.

docs.title: Travel times within a budget
docs.text:
max_fare keeps, for each pair, the fastest trip that costs no more than it:

o, d = points.iloc[:20], points.iloc[:200]
args = dict(mode=["WALK", "TRANSIT"], departure_datetime=departure,
            fare_structure=fares, draws_per_minute=1, n_threads=2)
cheap = peabiru.travel_time_matrix(network, o, d, max_fare=4.8, **args)
any_fare = peabiru.travel_time_matrix(network, o, d, **args)
both = cheap.merge(any_fare, on=["from_id", "to_id"], suffixes=("_4.8", "_any"))
print(both[["travel_time_p50_4.8", "travel_time_p50_any"]].mean().round(1).to_string())

travel_time_p50_4.8    61.2
travel_time_p50_any    52.2

With fares, McRAPTOR samples time_window * draws_per_minute departure times in the window instead of routing at every minute; the combinations its sampler cannot meet (exactly 200 draws, or too many for the window) are errors.

docs.title: The Pareto frontier
docs.text:
pareto_frontier() gives, for each pair, the travel time at each fare cutoff where it changes: the trade-off between time and money.

pf = peabiru.pareto_frontier(
    network, points.iloc[:1], points.iloc[:200], departure_datetime=departure,
    fare_structure=fares, fare_cutoffs=[4.5, 4.8, 8.37, 9.6], n_threads=2,
)
print(pf[pf["to_id"] == pf["to_id"].iloc[3]].to_string())

3  89a901291abffff  89a901295b7ffff          50           53           4.80
4  89a901291abffff  89a901295b7ffff          50           45           8.37

monetary_cost is the cutoff as the router reads it, a 32-bit float (4.8 is 4.800000190734863).

docs.title: GTFS errors
docs.text:
GTFS feeds often have errors: a trip that stops at a stop the feed does not have, two services with the same id, a time that cannot be read. get_gtfs_errors() lists them as the validator gtfs-lib (Conveyal) reports them, with every check of its table loaders and of its validation after loading, and build_network() refuses feeds with errors of priority "HIGH".

import shutil
import tempfile
import zipfile
from pathlib import Path

import peabiru

network = peabiru.build_network(peabiru.sample_data_path(), n_threads=2)
errors = peabiru.get_gtfs_errors(network)
print(errors.to_string())

       file  line               type       field   id priority
0    agency     3  DuplicateKeyError   agency_id    1   MEDIUM
1  calendar     8  DuplicateKeyError  service_id  USD   MEDIUM
2  calendar     9  DuplicateKeyError  service_id  U__   MEDIUM
3  calendar    10  DuplicateKeyError  service_id  US_   MEDIUM
4  calendar    11  DuplicateKeyError  service_id  _SD   MEDIUM
5  calendar    12  DuplicateKeyError  service_id  __D   MEDIUM
6  calendar    13  DuplicateKeyError  service_id  _S_   MEDIUM

Each row is one error: the table (file, without .txt), the line of the record (the header being line 1; 0 for a whole table), gtfs-lib's error class (type), the field and id involved (None when there is none) and the priority, "HIGH", "MEDIUM", "LOW" or "UNKNOWN". The rows are listed feed by feed, in the order gtfs-lib finds the errors. The feeds are read again on each call; nothing is written to the data directory.

docs.title: Feeds that are refused
docs.text:
A feed with errors of priority "HIGH" (a reference to a stop, route, trip, service or agency that does not exist, a number that cannot be read, tables in a subfolder of the .zip, routes without any agency) would be routed on broken data, so build_network() raises a RuntimeError that names the feeds. Here the first stop time of the sample feed is made to point to a stop that does not exist:

broken = Path(tempfile.mkdtemp())
sample = Path(peabiru.sample_data_path())
shutil.copy(sample / "spo_osm.pbf", broken)
with zipfile.ZipFile(sample / "spo_gtfs.zip") as zin, \
        zipfile.ZipFile(broken / "spo_gtfs.zip", "w") as zout:
    for name in zin.namelist():
        data = zin.read(name).decode("utf-8")
        if name == "stop_times.txt":
            header, first, rest = data.split("\n", 2)
            fields = first.split(",")
            fields[header.split(",").index("stop_id")] = "nowhere"
            data = "\n".join([header, ",".join(fields), rest])
        zout.writestr(name, data)

try:
    peabiru.build_network(broken, n_threads=2)
except RuntimeError as e:
    print(str(e).split(". Use")[0])

High priority GTFS errors found; network build failed (spo_gtfs.zip: 1 error)

The message points to get_gtfs_errors(), which also takes a directory of .zip files, so it works on feeds that cannot be built:

errors = peabiru.get_gtfs_errors(broken)
print(errors[errors["priority"] == "HIGH"].to_string())

         file  line                       type    field    id priority
7  stop_times     2  ReferentialIntegrityError  stop_id  None     HIGH

Fix the feed (here, the stop_id of line 2 of stop_times.txt) or remove the records at fault (with gtfs-kit in Python or gtfstools in R, for instance), and build the network again.

A feed on which gtfs-lib fails instead of listing errors (a date that is not YYYYMMDD, a frequency of a trip that does not exist, a service or fare without an id, the first or last stop of a trip without a name) makes both functions raise a RuntimeError naming the cause.

docs.title: Detailed itineraries
docs.text:
detailed_itineraries() gives the legs of each trip between pairs of origins and destinations: walking, cycling or driving, and each public transport ride, with its duration, waiting time, distance, route and line.

The examples use the sample data of Porto Alegre from the r5r project, downloaded once into the temporary directory (about 2 MB); its GTFS feeds only have service in the afternoon, hence the 14:00 departure.

import datetime as dt
import tempfile
import urllib.request
from pathlib import Path

import pandas as pd

import peabiru

poa = Path(tempfile.gettempdir()) / "peabiru-poa"
poa.mkdir(exist_ok=True)
url = "https://raw.githubusercontent.com/ipea/r5r/v2.5.0/r-package/inst/extdata/poa/"
for name in ["poa_osm.pbf", "poa_eptc.zip", "poa_trensurb.zip", "poa_points_of_interest.csv"]:
    if not (poa / name).exists():
        urllib.request.urlretrieve(url + name, poa / name)

network = peabiru.build_network(poa)  # a .pbf and GTFS .zip files
points = pd.read_csv(poa / "poa_points_of_interest.csv")  # id, lat, lon

trips = peabiru.detailed_itineraries(
    network, points.iloc[:3], points.iloc[3:6],
    mode=["WALK", "TRANSIT"],
    departure_datetime=dt.datetime(2019, 5, 13, 14, 0),
)
print(trips.drop(columns=["from_lat", "from_lon", "to_lat", "to_lon", "geometry"]).to_string())

Origins and destinations are paired row by row (a single origin or destination is repeated to match the other); all_to_all=True routes every origin to every destination. Each pair gets its fastest itinerary (shortest_path=True): the trip by the street mode alone, or the fastest public transport trip over the departure window, whichever is faster. Pairs without one have no rows.

The result is a geopandas.GeoDataFrame of LineStrings in EPSG:4326, one row per leg (segment), or a pandas.DataFrame with drop_geometry=True. Of note:

  • a street leg's line holds the whole of the first and last street segments, not only the parts walked or driven; the leg from the last stop ends at the destination itself;
  • a ride follows the GTFS shape of its trip pattern, or straight lines between stops when the feed has no shapes;
  • a walk between stops is routed again on the streets for its line and distance; its duration is the one public transport routing used.

docs.title: Alternatives
docs.text:
With shortest_path=False, each pair gets, besides the trip by the street mode alone, the alternatives the multi-criteria router (McRAPTOR) finds over the departure window, one per sequence of routes. suboptimal_minutes (which must be 0 with shortest_path=True) keeps search branches up to that many minutes slower than the best one, so higher values return more itineraries. The options are numbered by option in this order: the trip by the street mode alone first, then by the number of legs, then by duration, so the first option is not the fastest when a trip with fewer legs is slower (on Porto Alegre with suboptimal_minutes=10, a pair had 102 options, the first of 60.4 minutes and the fastest of 53.3):

def alternatives(minutes):
    return peabiru.detailed_itineraries(
        network, points.iloc[[1]], points.iloc[[4]],
        mode=["WALK", "TRANSIT"],
        departure_datetime=dt.datetime(2019, 5, 13, 14, 0),
        shortest_path=False, suboptimal_minutes=minutes, drop_geometry=True,
    )


for minutes in [0, 1, 5]:
    print(minutes, "minutes:", alternatives(minutes)["option"].nunique(), "options")
print(alternatives(0)[["option", "departure_time", "total_duration", "segment", "mode",

docs.title: Pairs
docs.text:
Origins and destinations are paired row by row, and a single origin or destination is repeated to match the other, with a warning; with all_to_all=True every origin is routed to every destination. The street examples below use the sample network of Sao Paulo, which is quicker to build:

import warnings

spo = peabiru.build_network(peabiru.sample_data_path(), n_threads=2)
spo_points = peabiru.sample_points()
pairs = peabiru.detailed_itineraries(
    spo, spo_points.iloc[:3], spo_points.iloc[3:6], mode="WALK",
    drop_geometry=True, n_threads=2,
)
every = peabiru.detailed_itineraries(
    spo, spo_points.iloc[:3], spo_points.iloc[3:6], mode="WALK",
    all_to_all=True, drop_geometry=True, n_threads=2,
)
with warnings.catch_warnings(record=True) as caught:
    warnings.simplefilter("always")
    one = peabiru.detailed_itineraries(
        spo, spo_points.iloc[:1], spo_points.iloc[3:6], mode="WALK",
        drop_geometry=True, n_threads=2,
    )
def n_pairs(trips):
    return len(trips[["from_id", "to_id"]].drop_duplicates())


print(n_pairs(pairs), "pairs;", n_pairs(every), "with all_to_all;", n_pairs(one), "from one origin")
print(caught[0].message)

3 pairs; 9 with all_to_all; 3 from one origin
'origins' was expanded to match the number of destinations.

With osm_link_ids=True (which needs the geometry, so not with drop_geometry=True), each street leg also lists the OpenStreetMap ways (osm_id_list) and the edges of the street network (edge_id_list, as street_network_to_sf() numbers them) it goes along, and each ride its board and alight stops (board_stop_id, alight_stop_id, as "<feed>:<stop_id>"). Consecutive edges on a roundabout give only their first ids, and connectors none:

bike = peabiru.detailed_itineraries(
    spo, spo_points.iloc[[0]], spo_points.iloc[[5]], mode="BICYCLE",
    osm_link_ids=True, n_threads=2,
)

docs.title: Car egress and turn restrictions
docs.text: With mode_egress="CAR", the egress is searched backwards from the destination, and a turn restriction with two or more via ways can be read in either order of those ways. peabiru fixes the order: every pair gets the itineraries of a freshly built network routing that pair alone with one thread, whatever the other pairs, the threads or the earlier calls, and a warning, once per call, names the pairs whose itineraries the other order of those via ways would change (on Porto Alegre, about 1 pair in 200). Rides along GTFS shapes are cut by shape_dist_traveled where the feed has it. Networks whose GTFS has frequency-based trips cannot be used with public transport here: convert the frequencies to stop times first (with gtfstools' frequencies_to_stop_times() in R, for instance).

docs.title: Inspecting a network
docs.text:
Five functions look into a network instead of routing on it: where points snap to the streets, the extent of the street network, the streets themselves, the public transport stops and routes, and the dates when public transport runs. The functions that return geometries need geopandas (pip install "peabiru[geo]"). The examples use the sample network:

import pandas as pd

import peabiru

network = peabiru.build_network(peabiru.sample_data_path(), n_threads=2)
points = peabiru.sample_points()

docs.title: Where points snap
docs.text:
Routing places each origin and destination on the nearest street the mode may use, looked for first within 300 metres of the point and then, if there is none, within radius (1,600 m by default). A point that does not snap is not routed. find_snap() shows where each point snaps, and how far away:

snaps = peabiru.find_snap(network, points, mode="CAR")
print(snaps.head(3).to_string())

1  89a8100c007ffff -23.557703 -46.632067 -23.558186 -46.632041  53.681610   True
2  89a8100c077ffff -23.553245 -46.628874 -23.553252 -46.628872   0.768439   True

The street a point snaps to depends on the mode, since some streets cannot be used by some modes (a pedestrian street cannot be used to snap car trips). A point too far from every street has found False and NaN coordinates:

far = pd.DataFrame({"id": ["far away"], "lon": [-46.70], "lat": [-23.60]})
print(peabiru.find_snap(network, far).to_string())
