docs.title: build_network
docs.text:
build_network(data_path: PathLike, verbose: bool = False, temp_dir: bool = False, elevation: str = 'TOBLER', overwrite: bool = False, n_threads: Optional[Union[int, float]] = math.inf) -> Network

Build a transport network.

Builds a multimodal transport network from a directory with one OpenStreetMap extract (.pbf) and zero or more GTFS feeds (.zip), and optionally an elevation raster (.tif). The network lives in memory and is reused by every routing function; nothing is written to data_path. The files are recognised by their extension in lower case only: a map.PBF or a feed.ZIP is ignored.

A .tif raster in data_path gives walking and cycling times slope costs (elevation="TOBLER", the default, or "MINETTI"; never for cars): the raster is sampled every 10 m along each street at the nearest pixel, and each street's time is multiplied by the average cost of its slopes. Points outside the raster count as 0 m high. Without a .tif raster the network is built with elevation="NONE".

The raster must be a GeoTIFF with one band, north up, uncompressed or compressed with LZW, Deflate or PackBits (what GDAL writes by default), in WGS 84 longitude and latitude (EPSG:4326) or in another coordinate reference system whose transform peabiru reproduces exactly, given by its EPSG code (what GDAL writes): SIRGAS 2000 (4674), SAD69 (4618), Corrego Alegre 1970-72 (4225), their UTM zones used in Brazil (31965-31985, 6210, 6211, 5396; 29168-29172, 29187-29195; 22521-22525), SIRGAS 2000 / Brazil Polyconic (5880), WGS 84 / UTM (32601-32660, 32701-32760) and WGS 84 / Pseudo-Mercator (3857). Other rasters are an error that says what to change, and so are a .prj file next to the raster, a raster whose name ends in .tiff and more than one raster.

In a projected system, a street point within nanometres (5e-8 m, or 2e-13 degrees) of the boundary between two pixels of different values, or of the raster's edge, reads the pixel that peabiru's own sines and cosines give, the same on every machine, and a UserWarning gives the number of such points (about one in a hundred million for 30 m pixels; reprojecting the raster to EPSG:4326 removes the ambiguity). A point that falls on the raster's outer edge (inside its envelope, past the last pixel) is an error: there is no pixel to read. Elevations are kept in decimetres in 16-bit integers, so voids and values beyond +/-3276.7 m wrap around (SRTM's -32768 voids become 0 m, -9999 becomes 3108.2 m, a NaN no-data value becomes 0 m); a UserWarning counts them and the samples equal to the raster's no-data value. A routing call with a scenario (new_carspeeds, carspeed_scale, new_lts) on a network with elevation runs without the slope costs, with a warning. See Elevation.

The GTFS feeds are loaded in the order in which the operating system lists the directory. With more than one feed that order depends on the file system, so the same directory can give slightly different expanded and arrival matrices on two machines (another stop or route for a few trips); on one machine the results are always the same.

The network is not built when a GTFS feed has errors of priority "HIGH" (a reference to a stop, route, trip, service or agency that does not exist, a number that cannot be read, tables in a subfolder of the .zip, routes without any agency): the RuntimeError names the feeds and points to get_gtfs_errors(), which lists the errors. A feed that cannot be loaded at all is an error too.

Parameters:

Name Type Description Default data_path str or PathLike

The directory with the .pbf file, the GTFS feeds and the elevation raster.

required verbose bool

Whether to report the build of the network (on standard error).

False temp_dir bool

Only checked; it has no effect (see the Notes).

False elevation ('TOBLER', 'MINETTI', 'NONE')

The slope cost function for walking and cycling when data_path has a .tif elevation raster: Tobler's hiking function, Minetti's energy cost of walking, or no slope costs. Case does not matter.

"TOBLER" overwrite bool

Only checked; it has no effect: the network is always built anew.

False n_threads int or inf

The number of threads used to read the .pbf file; math.inf (or None) uses all cores.

math.inf

Returns:

Type Description Network

The network to pass to the routing functions.

Raises:

Type Description ValueError

When data_path has no .pbf file or more than one, or elevation is not one of the choices.

RuntimeError

When a file cannot be read, a GTFS feed has errors of priority "HIGH", or the elevation raster is not one peabiru reads.

Notes

Nothing is written to data_path; temp_dir and overwrite are checked and have no effect (there is no file to keep or to rebuild). More than one .pbf file is an error. In a projected raster, the pixel read for a point within nanometres of a pixel boundary is the same on every machine, with a warning that counts such points.

Examples:

>>> import peabiru
>>> network = peabiru.build_network(peabiru.sample_data_path(), n_threads=2)
>>> network.info()["feeds"]
['spo_gtfs']

travel_time_matrix(network: Network, origins: DataFrame, destinations: DataFrame, mode: Mode = 'WALK', mode_egress: str = 'WALK', departure_datetime: Optional[Any] = None, time_window: Number = 10, percentiles: Union[int, Sequence[int]] = 50, max_walk_time: Number = math.inf, max_bike_time: Number = math.inf, max_car_time: Number = math.inf, max_trip_duration: Number = 120, walk_speed: float = 3.6, bike_speed: float = 12, max_rides: Number = 3, max_lts: Number = 2, fare_structure: Any = None, max_fare: Number = math.inf, new_carspeeds: Optional[Any] = None, carspeed_scale: float = 1, new_lts: Optional[Any] = None, draws_per_minute: Number = 5, seed: Optional[Number] = None, n_threads: Optional[Number] = math.inf, verbose: bool = False, progress: bool = True, output_dir: Optional[PathArg] = None) -> Union[pd.DataFrame, PathArg]

Travel-time matrix between origins and destinations.

Travel times between every origin and every destination, by one street mode ("WALK", "BICYCLE" or "CAR") or by public transport (all of it or some of its modes, reached and left on foot, by bicycle or by car). With public transport, the travel time from an origin to a destination is computed for every departure minute of the time window (and every Monte Carlo draw with frequency-based GTFS), and the result reports percentiles of those times.

A bicycle or car trip to public transport goes on on foot from wherever the vehicle got, within the same max_bike_time or max_car_time, and the trip without public transport keeps those walking ends too. Egress by bicycle or car is searched from every stop with fixed limits (up to 5 km by bicycle at any level of traffic stress, up to 30 minutes by car) and must stay within max_bike_time or max_car_time.

Parameters:

Name Type Description Default network Network

A network built with build_network().

required origins DataFrame

Points with columns id, lon and lat (WGS 84), or a geopandas.GeoDataFrame of points in EPSG:4326 with an id column. Ids that are not strings are converted with str(), with a warning; points with missing coordinates are not routed, with a warning; duplicated ids are an error.

required destinations DataFrame

Points, as origins.

required mode str or sequence of str

One of "WALK", "BICYCLE" or "CAR", and for public transport "TRANSIT" (every transit mode) or any of "TRAM", "SUBWAY", "RAIL", "BUS", "FERRY", "CABLE_CAR", "GONDOLA" and "FUNICULAR"; the street mode (walking by default) reaches public transport.

"WALK" mode_egress str

The mode from the last stop to the destination: "WALK", "BICYCLE" or "CAR".

"WALK" departure_datetime datetime

The departure date and time. Its date and clock time are taken as they read, in its own time zone when it is timezone-aware. Required with transit.

None time_window int

The window of departure minutes, starting at departure_datetime, over which travel times are computed.

10 percentiles int or sequence of int

Up to 5 distinct values from 1 to 99, the travel-time percentiles over the time window to report.

50 max_walk_time int or float

The maximum walking time in minutes (math.inf means the trip limit).

math.inf max_bike_time int or float

The maximum cycling time in minutes (math.inf means the trip limit).

math.inf max_car_time int or float

The maximum driving time in minutes (math.inf means the trip limit).

math.inf max_trip_duration int

The maximum trip duration in minutes.

120 walk_speed float

Walking speed in km/h.

3.6 bike_speed float

Cycling speed in km/h.

12 max_rides int

The maximum number of public transport rides.

3 max_lts int

The highest level of traffic stress (1 to 4) a cyclist will ride on.

2 fare_structure dict

A fare structure (see setup_fare_structure()). With one, public transport is routed with fares by the multi-criteria router (McRAPTOR), over time_window * draws_per_minute departure times sampled in the window, and max_fare limits what a trip may cost (see Fares).

None max_fare float

The highest fare a trip may cost; a finite value needs a fare_structure.

math.inf new_carspeeds DataFrame or GeoDataFrame

A scenario of car speeds (see Scenarios): a DataFrame with columns osm_id, max_speed and speed_type ("scale", a factor for the car speed of the way's edges, or "km/h", a speed; 0 closes the way to cars), or a GeoDataFrame of polygons in WGS 84 with columns poly_id (str), scale and priority (int): each street edge takes the factor of the polygon it meets with the highest priority (ties: the one it overlaps most).

None carspeed_scale float

The factor for the car speeds of the edges new_carspeeds leaves out (all of them when it is None).

1 new_lts DataFrame or GeoDataFrame

A scenario of levels of traffic stress: a DataFrame with columns osm_id and lts (int), or a GeoDataFrame of lines in WGS 84 with columns line_id, lts (1 to 4) and priority: each street edge takes the level of the line closest to it among those whose bounding box meets its own. A scenario changes the street search from the origins (the trip without public transport, access by bicycle or car) but not the egress from the stops, and a network with elevation is routed without its slope costs, with a warning. A car speed that would become 0 or less, or pass the range of the 16-bit cm/s speeds are kept in, a polygon that is not valid, and a tie with no winner (two polygons of the same priority and different scales that overlap a way by the same length) are errors.

None draws_per_minute int

The Monte Carlo draws per departure minute for frequency-based GTFS.

5 seed int

A seed for the Monte Carlo draws. With frequency-based GTFS, results are reproducible only with a seed.

None n_threads int or inf

The number of threads; math.inf (or None) uses all cores.

math.inf verbose bool

Only checked; it has no effect.

False progress bool

Only checked; peabiru prints no progress counter.

True output_dir str or PathLike

An existing directory: instead of returning the result, write it there, one CSV file per origin named from_<origin id>.csv (see Writing results to files), and return output_dir. Origins are routed a slice at a time, so the whole result is never held in memory. The file names are built from the ids: an id that cannot name a file there (with a path separator or NUL; on Windows also < > : " | ? *) raises ValueError before anything is routed.

None

Returns:

Type Description DataFrame or str or PathLike

With output_dir, output_dir itself. Otherwise: from_id, to_id (strings, object dtype) and one Int32 column travel_time_pXX per percentile, ascending (minutes). Rows are origin-major, in input order. Pairs that cannot be completed within max_trip_duration are not returned; a higher percentile beyond the limit is <NA>.

Notes

With a seed, the Monte Carlo draws of frequency-based GTFS are reproducible.

Examples:

>>> import datetime as dt
>>> import peabiru
>>> network = peabiru.build_network(peabiru.sample_data_path(), n_threads=2)
>>> points = peabiru.sample_points()
>>> ttm = peabiru.travel_time_matrix(
...     network, points, points,
...     mode=["WALK", "TRANSIT"],
...     departure_datetime=dt.datetime(2019, 5, 13, 14, 0),
...     percentiles=[25, 50, 75],
...     seed=42,
...     n_threads=2,
... )
>>> list(ttm.columns)
['from_id', 'to_id', 'travel_time_p25', 'travel_time_p50', 'travel_time_p75']

isochrone(network: Network, origins: DataFrame, mode: Mode = 'transit', mode_egress: str = 'walk', cutoffs: Union[Number, Sequence[Number]] = (0, 15, 30), zoom: Number = 10, departure_datetime: Optional[Any] = None, polygon_output: bool = True, time_window: Number = 10, max_walk_time: Number = math.inf, max_bike_time: Number = math.inf, max_car_time: Number = math.inf, max_trip_duration: Number = 120, walk_speed: float = 3.6, bike_speed: float = 12, max_rides: Number = 3, max_lts: Number = 2, draws_per_minute: Number = 5, seed: Optional[Number] = None, percentiles: Optional[Union[int, Sequence[int]]] = None, n_threads: Optional[Number] = math.inf, verbose: bool = False, progress: bool = True) -> Any

Isochrones: the areas or street segments reached from each origin.

The areas (polygon_output=True) or the street segments (polygon_output=False) reached from each origin within each cutoff, by one street mode ("WALK", "BICYCLE" or "CAR") or by public transport (see travel_time_matrix()).

Polygon isochrones are made from travel times from each origin to the centres of a regular grid of Web Mercator pixels covering the network (see zoom): the band from 0 to each cutoff is traced over the grid by marching squares and grouped into polygons with holes, as the R package isoband does (a port of it, vertex for vertex). The geometries are MultiPolygons (shells as traced, holes reversed); pass them to shapely.make_valid() if your tools need valid geometries (rings of one polygon may touch at a vertex).

Line isochrones are the travel times from each origin to the centroid of every street segment of street_network_to_sf(), each segment in the band of the smallest cutoff at or above its travel time.

max_trip_duration is ignored: the trip limit is the largest cutoff (plus 10 minutes for polygons, so that the outer band is interpolated like the inner ones).

Needs geopandas (pip install 'peabiru[geo]').

Parameters:

Name Type Description Default network Network

A network built with build_network().

required origins DataFrame

Points with columns id, lon and lat (WGS 84), or a geopandas.GeoDataFrame of points in EPSG:4326 with an id column, as in travel_time_matrix().

required mode str or sequence of str

One of "WALK", "BICYCLE" or "CAR", and for public transport "TRANSIT" (every transit mode) or any of "TRAM", "SUBWAY", "RAIL", "BUS", "FERRY", "CABLE_CAR", "GONDOLA" and "FUNICULAR"; the street mode (walking by default) reaches public transport; case does not matter.

"transit" mode_egress str

The mode from the last stop to the destination: "WALK", "BICYCLE" or "CAR".

"walk" cutoffs number or sequence of numbers

The travel times in minutes that delimit the isochrones: finite and at least 0. They are sorted and duplicates removed; 0 is added, and at least one must be greater than 0.

(0, 15, 30) zoom int

From 9 to 12: the Web Mercator zoom level of the travel-time grid polygons are interpolated from (cells of about 153 metres at the Equator at zoom 10). Only used for polygons.

10 departure_datetime datetime

The departure date and time, as in travel_time_matrix(). Required with transit.

None polygon_output bool

True for polygons, False for the street segments reached.

True time_window int

The window of departure minutes over which travel times are computed.

10 max_walk_time int or float

The maximum walking time in minutes (math.inf means the trip limit).

math.inf max_bike_time int or float

The maximum cycling time in minutes.

math.inf max_car_time int or float

The maximum driving time in minutes.

math.inf max_trip_duration int

Ignored: the trip limit comes from the cutoffs.

120 walk_speed float

Walking speed in km/h.

3.6 bike_speed float

Cycling speed in km/h.

12 max_rides int

The maximum number of public transport rides.

3 max_lts int

The highest level of traffic stress (1 to 4) a cyclist will ride on.

2 draws_per_minute int

The Monte Carlo draws per departure minute for frequency-based GTFS.

5 seed int

A seed for the Monte Carlo draws; with frequency-based GTFS the results are reproducible only with a seed.

None percentiles int or sequence of int

Up to 5 distinct values from 1 to 99: the travel-time percentiles to make polygons for. None (the default) means 50. Must be None for line isochrones.

None n_threads int or inf

The number of threads; math.inf (or None) uses all cores.

math.inf verbose bool

Only checked; it has no effect.

False progress bool

Only checked; peabiru prints no progress counter.

True

Returns:

Type Description GeoDataFrame

In EPSG:4326. With polygon_output=True: id, isochrone (the cutoff, float), percentile (such as "p50") and the geometry column polygons (a MultiPolygon, empty when nothing is reached), one row per origin, percentile (ascending) and cutoff (descending). With polygon_output=False: id, edge_index (a string), osm_id (int64), isochrone, travel_time_p50 (Int32), the segment's from_vertex, to_vertex, street_class, length (metres), walk, car, car_speed (km/h), bicycle, bicycle_lts and the geometry column geometry (a LineString); rows by origin, then by band and travel time, both descending.

Notes

The travel times are those of travel_time_matrix(). The polygons are contoured with the isoband algorithm, whose rings follow the C++ library isoband is built with on each platform (libc++ on macOS, libstdc++ on Linux and Windows). They are returned as contoured, always as MultiPolygons, and are not made valid: pass them to shapely.make_valid() if your tools need valid geometries. Line isochrones route to the centroids of the street segments.

Examples:

>>> import datetime as dt
>>> import peabiru
>>> network = peabiru.build_network(peabiru.sample_data_path(), n_threads=2)
>>> origin = peabiru.sample_points().iloc[:1]
>>> iso = peabiru.isochrone(
...     network, origin, mode="WALK", cutoffs=[0, 10, 20],
...     departure_datetime=dt.datetime(2019, 5, 13, 14, 0), n_threads=2,
... )
>>> list(iso.columns), list(iso.isochrone)
(['id', 'isochrone', 'percentile', 'polygons'], [20.0, 10.0])

Detailed itineraries between origin-destination pairs.

The itinerary of each trip between pairs of origins and destinations: its legs (walking, cycling, driving and each ride), with their duration, waiting time, distance, route and line. Each pair gets the trip by the street mode alone and, with public transport, the fastest trip over the departure window (shortest_path=True: only the fastest of all is kept) or, with shortest_path=False, the alternatives the multi-criteria router (McRAPTOR) finds, one per sequence of routes (more of them with suboptimal_minutes). With a fare_structure, the trips are routed with fares and get total_fare and cumulative_fare columns (see Fares).

Networks whose GTFS has frequency-based trips cannot be used with public transport here. With mode_egress="CAR", a pair whose egress crosses a turn restriction with two or more via ways, which can be read in either order, gets the itineraries of a freshly built network routing that pair alone, with a warning; see Detailed itineraries.

setup_fare_structure(network: Network, base_fare: Number, by: str = 'MODE', debug_path: Optional[str] = None, debug_info: Optional[str] = None) -> FareStructure

Set up a fare structure to calculate the monetary costs of trips.

Every route, fare type and transfer between two types costs base_fare (read as a 32-bit float), with one fare type per mode (by="MODE"), per agency ("AGENCY_ID", "AGENCY_NAME") or one for all routes ("GENERIC"). Edit the result to follow the fare rules of the study area, and pass it to the routing functions as fare_structure (see Fares).

Name Type Description Default network Network

A network built with build_network().

required base_fare float

The fare of every route, type and transfer, at least 0.

required by ('MODE', 'AGENCY_ID', 'AGENCY_NAME', 'GENERIC')

What a fare type groups: the routes of a mode, of an agency (by id or by name), or all routes. Case does not matter.

"MODE" debug_path str

Debug settings, kept in debug_settings: a .csv path and "MODE", "ROUTE" (the default with a debug_path) or "MODE_ROUTE". No debug file is written.

None debug_info str

Debug settings, kept in debug_settings: a .csv path and "MODE", "ROUTE" (the default with a debug_path) or "MODE_ROUTE". No debug file is written.

None

The fare structure: max_discounted_transfers (1), transfer_time_allowance (120 minutes), fare_cap (inf), the DataFrames fares_per_type (type, unlimited_transfers, allow_same_route_transfer, use_route_fare, fare), fares_per_transfer (first_leg, second_leg, fare) and fares_per_route (agency_id, agency_name, route_id, route_short_name, route_long_name, mode, route_fare, fare_type), and debug_settings (a dict with output_file and trip_info).

The debug settings are kept in the structure, but no debug file is written.

>>> import peabiru

['BUS', 'RAIL', 'SUBWAY']

[4.4, 4.4, 4.4]

Trip options between origin-destination pairs.

For each pair of origin and destination, every trip worth considering: the trips that no other trip beats on all the chosen criteria at once. This is peabiru's own multi-criteria trip planner; see the guide Trip options for the definitions, a worked example, and how it differs from pareto_frontier() and detailed_itineraries().

A trip dominates another when it is no worse on every chosen criterion and better on at least one. At each departure minute of the window the options are the exact set of trips not dominated (one per combination of values; of trips equal on the chosen criteria, the one with the least total time, then transfers, minutes on foot and fare), compared with total time to a tenth of a minute and walking to the minute (walk_resolution), so that trips a few seconds apart are not all returned; the search is exact and the values returned are exact. The minutes are merged into options: trips with the same street modes, the same routes between the same stops and the same fare, transfers and minutes on foot are one option, reported at its best minute (the least total time). Frequency-based routes are boarded at their expected times (half a headway of waiting; the scheduled departures with exact_times = 1): no random draws, no seed.

docs.text:
locate_facilities(network: Any, demand: Any, candidates: Any, existing: Any = None, model: str = 'max_cover', n_facilities: Any = 1, cutoff: Any = None, demand_colname: Optional[str] = None, mode: Any = 'WALK', mode_egress: str = 'WALK', departure_datetime: Optional[Any] = None, percentile: Any = 50, max_trip_duration: Any = None, travel_times: Any = None, swap: bool = True, min_gain: Any = 0, unreachable_time: Any = None, n_threads: Any = None, **routing: Any) -> FacilityLocation

Where to open new facilities.

Chooses, among the candidate sites, where to open facilities so that the demand points are served best, by one of four classic location models. The travel times from every demand point to every site are computed with travel_time_matrix() (or taken from travel_times), so any mode, departure time and routing option of the matrix applies.

The models:

  • "max_cover", maximal covering: with n_facilities new facilities, cover the most demand within cutoff minutes.
  • "set_cover", location set covering: the fewest new facilities that leave every demand point within cutoff minutes of one (every point some site can cover; the others are reported).
  • "p_median": n_facilities new facilities with the smallest demand-weighted sum of travel times to the nearest facility.
  • "p_center": n_facilities new facilities with the smallest travel time for the demand point farthest from its nearest facility.

The existing facilities are already open and count first: only the demand they leave uncovered, or the travel time they leave, drives the choice of the new sites.

The models are solved by heuristics: a greedy construction (each site the one that improves the objective most, given the ones before it) followed, with swap, by vertex substitution (swap an open new site for a closed candidate while that improves the objective). The solution is good and reproducible, not proven optimal; for maximal covering the greedy solution covers at least 63% (1 - 1/e) of the most that could be covered of the demand not yet covered. Ties go to the candidate listed first, and the result does not depend on n_threads. See the guide Facility location.

Parameters:

Name Type Description Default network Network or None

The network of build_network(); may be None with travel_times.

required demand DataFrame or GeoDataFrame

The demand points: id, lon, lat (or point geometries in WGS 84) and, with demand_colname, their weights.

required candidates DataFrame or GeoDataFrame

The sites where a facility could open: id, lon, lat.

required existing DataFrame or GeoDataFrame

The facilities already open: id, lon, lat. Their ids may not repeat those of the candidates.

None model str

"max_cover", "set_cover", "p_median" or "p_center".

"max_cover" n_facilities int

How many new facilities to open. Fewer come back when no further site improves the objective. Ignored by "set_cover".

1 cutoff number

The service standard of the covering models, in minutes: a point is covered by a site at most this far (travel time <= cutoff). Required by "max_cover" and "set_cover".

None demand_colname str

The column of demand with the weight of each point (residents, pupils...): finite and not negative. Without it every point weighs 1. In "set_cover" and "p_center" a point with weight 0 is not demand, and the others count the same.

None mode Any

How the demand points travel to the sites, as in travel_time_matrix() (default: on foot).

'WALK' mode_egress Any

How the demand points travel to the sites, as in travel_time_matrix() (default: on foot).

'WALK' departure_datetime Any

How the demand points travel to the sites, as in travel_time_matrix() (default: on foot).

'WALK' percentile int

The travel-time percentile used (public transport over a time window).

50 max_trip_duration int

The longest trip considered, in minutes. Default: cutoff (rounded up) for the covering models, 120 for the others. A demand point farther than this from every facility counts as reaching none.

None travel_times DataFrame

A table of travel times to use instead of routing: from_id (demand point), to_id (site) and travel_time_pXX for the percentile (or travel_time), in minutes, as travel_time_matrix() returns it. A pair that is absent or has a missing time is unreachable; rows of other points are ignored. With it, network and the routing arguments are not used and the points need only their id.

None swap bool

Improve the greedy solution by vertex substitution (for "set_cover", drop the sites the others make redundant).

True min_gain number

"max_cover" stops opening sites when the best one left would cover less than this much demand.

0 unreachable_time number

For "p_median" and "p_center", the minutes charged to a demand point that reaches no open facility. Default: twice the longest travel time of the table.

None n_threads int

Threads (default: all cores).

None **routing Any

Any other argument of travel_time_matrix(): time_window, walk_speed, max_walk_time, seed and so on (not percentiles or output_dir).

{}

Returns:

Type Description FacilityLocation

Four tables: sites, candidates, demand and summary (see FacilityLocation).

Examples:

Two new schools among the 27 sample points, so that the most residents are within a 12-minute walk of a school:

>>> import peabiru
>>> network = peabiru.build_network(peabiru.sample_data_path())
>>> points = peabiru.sample_points()
>>> schools = points[points["schools"] > 0]
>>> others = points[points["schools"] == 0]
>>> found = peabiru.locate_facilities(
...     network, points, others, existing=schools,
...     model="max_cover", n_facilities=2, cutoff=12,
...     demand_colname="population", mode="WALK",
... )
>>> list(found.sites.columns)
['id', 'lon', 'lat', 'order', 'marginal', 'cumulative']
>>> list(found.sites["id"])
['89a8100c03bffff', '89a8100c383ffff']
>>> found.summary["covered_before"], found.summary["covered"]
(37876.0, 46217.0)

floating_catchment(network: Any, demand: Any, supply: Any, cutoff: Any = None, decay_function: str = 'step', decay_value: Optional[float] = None, demand_colname: Optional[str] = None, supply_colname: Optional[str] = None, mode: Any = 'WALK', mode_egress: str = 'WALK', departure_datetime: Optional[Any] = None, percentile: Any = 50, max_trip_duration: Any = None, travel_times: Any = None, **routing: Any) -> FloatingCatchment

Supply against demand around each place: the two-step floating catchment area.

Step 1: the supply of each facility (places, staff, beds) is divided by the demand within its catchment. Step 2: each demand point adds up the ratios of the facilities within its catchment. The result, per demand point, is supply per unit of demand, which accounts both for how near the facilities are and for how many others compete for them.

With decay_function="step" a pair of demand point and facility counts in full up to cutoff minutes and not at all beyond: the two-step floating catchment area in its original form. Any other decay function gives the enhanced form, in which nearer pairs weigh more, in both steps; the functions and their values are those of accessibility().

The sum over the demand points of demand times accessibility equals the supply of the facilities that have any demand in their catchment.

Find where points snap to the street network.

Snapping is how routing places origins and destinations on the network. The nearest point of a street the mode may use is looked for first within 300 metres of the point and then, if there is none, within radius. A point that does not snap is not routed. The street a point snaps to depends on the mode, since some streets cannot be used by some modes (a pedestrian street cannot be used to snap car trips).

docs.text:
get_gtfs_errors(network: Union[Network, PathLike]) -> pd.DataFrame

The errors gtfs-lib reports in the network's GTFS feeds.

The errors that the validator gtfs-lib (Conveyal) reports when it reads the feeds, with every check of gtfs-lib's table loaders and of its post-load validation. build_network() refuses feeds with errors of priority "HIGH"; this function lists them, from the files a network was built from or from the .zip files of a directory (so it also works on feeds that cannot be built). The feeds are read again on each call; the rows are listed feed by feed, in the order gtfs-lib finds them.

A feed on which gtfs-lib fails instead of listing errors (a date that is not YYYYMMDD, a frequency of a trip that does not exist, a service or fare without an id, the first or last stop of a trip without a name) raises RuntimeError naming the cause, and so does a locations.geojson of GTFS-Flex zones that is not in UTF-8. GTFS-Flex zones and location groups are read as gtfs-lib reads them, for its errors; on-demand trips are not routed.

Parameters:

Name Type Description Default network (Network, str or PathLike)

A network built with build_network(), or a directory with GTFS feeds (.zip).

required

Returns:

Type Description DataFrame

file (the table, without .txt), line (the record, the header being line 1; 0 for a whole table), type (gtfs-lib's error class), field and id (None when the error has none) and priority ("HIGH", "MEDIUM", "LOW" or "UNKNOWN").

Notes

The feeds are read again at each call, and the rows are listed feed by feed in the order the errors are found, the same in every run. A directory that does not exist is an error.

Examples:

>>> import peabiru
>>> network = peabiru.build_network(peabiru.sample_data_path(), n_threads=2)
>>> errors = peabiru.get_gtfs_errors(network)
>>> sorted(set(errors["type"]))
['DuplicateKeyError']

docs.title: Scenarios
docs.text:
The routing functions take three arguments that change the street network for one call, without building it again:

  • new_carspeeds: new car speeds, by OpenStreetMap way or inside polygons;
  • carspeed_scale: a factor for the car speeds of every other street;
  • new_lts: new levels of traffic stress (LTS) for cycling, by OpenStreetMap way or near lines.

They are accepted by travel_time_matrix(), accessibility(), expanded_travel_time_matrix(), arrival_travel_time_matrix() and detailed_itineraries(). A scenario changes the street search from the origins (the trip without public transport, and access to it by bicycle or car) but not the egress from the stops. The examples use the sample network; the OpenStreetMap ids come from its primary roads:

import geopandas as gpd
import pandas as pd

import peabiru

network = peabiru.build_network(peabiru.sample_data_path(), n_threads=2)
points = peabiru.sample_points()
edges = peabiru.street_network_to_sf(network)["edges"]
primary = edges[edges["street_class"] == "PRIMARY"]
primary_ids = primary["osm_id"].unique()


def summary(mode, **scenario):
    """Pairs reached and their mean travel time, by one street mode."""
    ttm = peabiru.travel_time_matrix(network, points, points, mode=mode,
                                     n_threads=2, **scenario)
    return len(ttm), round(float(ttm["travel_time_p50"].astype(float).mean()), 2)


print(len(primary_ids), "primary ways;", "by car:", summary("CAR"))

88 primary ways; by car: (729, 7.46)

docs.title: Car speeds by way
docs.text:
new_carspeeds as a DataFrame has columns osm_id, max_speed and speed_type. With speed_type="scale", max_speed multiplies the car speed of the way's edges; with "km/h" it replaces it. A value of 0 closes the way to cars. carspeed_scale multiplies the speeds of the edges new_carspeeds leaves out (all of them without new_carspeeds):

slower = pd.DataFrame({"osm_id": primary_ids, "max_speed": 0.5, "speed_type": "scale"})
at_20 = pd.DataFrame({"osm_id": primary_ids, "max_speed": 20.0, "speed_type": "km/h"})
closed = pd.DataFrame({"osm_id": primary_ids, "max_speed": 0.0, "speed_type": "scale"})
print("primary roads at half speed:", summary("CAR", new_carspeeds=slower))
print("primary roads at 20 km/h:   ", summary("CAR", new_carspeeds=at_20))
print("primary roads closed:       ", summary("CAR", new_carspeeds=closed))
print("every street at 80%:        ", summary("CAR", carspeed_scale=0.8))
print("20 km/h, the rest at 80%:   ", summary("CAR", new_carspeeds=at_20, carspeed_scale=0.8))

primary roads at half speed: (729, 7.54)
primary roads at 20 km/h:    (729, 7.6)
primary roads closed:        (651, 7.52)
every street at 80%:         (729, 8.14)
20 km/h, the rest at 80%:    (729, 8.26)

With the primary roads closed, one of the points, which snaps to one of them, can only reach itself by car, and so 78 pairs are lost.

docs.title: Car speeds in polygons
docs.text:
new_carspeeds as a GeoDataFrame of polygons in WGS 84 has columns poly_id (strings), scale (a factor) and priority (integers). Each street edge takes the factor of the polygon it meets with the highest priority (ties: the one it overlaps most); carspeed_scale applies to the edges outside every polygon:

bbox = peabiru.street_network_bbox(network, "vector")
centre = gpd.points_from_xy([(bbox["xmin"] + bbox["xmax"]) / 2],
                            [(bbox["ymin"] + bbox["ymax"]) / 2])
zone = gpd.GeoDataFrame(
    {"poly_id": ["centre"], "scale": [0.3], "priority": [1]},
    geometry=centre.buffer(0.005),  # about 500 m around the centre
    crs="EPSG:4326",
)
print("30% of the speed within 500 m of the centre:", summary("CAR", new_carspeeds=zone))

30% of the speed within 500 m of the centre: (729, 9.66)

docs.title: Levels of traffic stress
docs.text:
max_lts (2 by default) is the highest level of traffic stress, from 1 to 4, a cyclist rides on. new_lts changes the level of streets: as a DataFrame with columns osm_id and lts (integers), or as a GeoDataFrame of lines in WGS 84 with columns line_id, lts (1 to 4) and priority, where each street edge takes the level of the line closest to it among those whose bounding box meets its own:

calm = pd.DataFrame({"osm_id": primary_ids, "lts": 1})
lanes = gpd.GeoDataFrame(
    {"line_id": primary["edge_index"].astype(str), "lts": 1, "priority": 1},
    geometry=primary.geometry.values,
    crs="EPSG:4326",
)
print("by bicycle:                 ", summary("BICYCLE"))
print("primary roads at LTS 1:     ", summary("BICYCLE", new_lts=calm))
print("cycle lanes along them:     ", summary("BICYCLE", new_lts=lanes))

by bicycle:                  (729, 11.82)
primary roads at LTS 1:      (729, 11.21)
cycle lanes along them:      (729, 10.87)

The lines lower the stress of more streets than the way ids do: an edge takes the level of the closest line whose bounding box meets its own, so the streets next to a primary road, whose bounding boxes meet a line's, get level 1 too.

docs.title: What is an error
docs.text:
Car speeds are kept as 16-bit integers of centimetres per second. A scenario that does not fit them is an error rather than a result:

  • a car speed that would pass that range or come to 0 or less (a negative factor or speed, a polygon scale of math.inf or 0, a carspeed_scale far above 1), and a carspeed_scale beyond the 32-bit float range;
  • a carspeed_scale of NaN;
  • a polygon that is not valid, and a tie with no winner: two polygons of the same priority and different scales that overlap a way by the same length (give one of them a higher priority).
backwards = pd.DataFrame({"osm_id": primary_ids, "max_speed": -1.0, "speed_type": "scale"})
try:
    summary("CAR", new_carspeeds=backwards)
except ValueError as e:
    print(str(e)[:72], "...")

the scenario leaves 140 street edges open to cars with a speed of 0 or l ...

On a network with an elevation raster, a call with a scenario runs without the slope costs, with a warning (see Elevation).

docs.title: Travel-time matrices
docs.text:
travel_time_matrix() computes the travel time from every origin to every destination, by a street mode or by public transport. The examples on this page use the sample network:

import datetime as dt

import pandas as pd

import peabiru

network = peabiru.build_network(peabiru.sample_data_path(), n_threads=2)
points = peabiru.sample_points()

docs.title: Street modes
docs.text:
With one street mode, "WALK", "BICYCLE" or "CAR", the result has one row per pair that can be reached within max_trip_duration (120 minutes by default), in origin-major order, following the order of the input points:

car = peabiru.travel_time_matrix(network, points, points, mode="CAR", n_threads=2)
print(car.head(3))
print(car.dtypes)

           from_id            to_id  travel_time_p50
0  89a8100c00fffff  89a8100c00fffff                2
1  89a8100c00fffff  89a8100c007ffff                4
2  89a8100c00fffff  89a8100c077ffff                2
from_id            object
to_id              object
travel_time_p50     Int32
dtype: object

from_id and to_id are strings (object dtype); travel times are whole minutes in pandas' nullable Int32. Speeds and limits are arguments:

bike = peabiru.travel_time_matrix(
    network, points, points,
    mode="BICYCLE",
    bike_speed=15,         # km/h
    max_lts=3,             # highest level of traffic stress, 1 to 4
    max_bike_time=10,      # minutes
    n_threads=2,
)
print(len(bike), "pairs within 10 minutes;", bike["travel_time_p50"].max(), "at most")

406 pairs within 10 minutes; 10 at most

A street trip has one travel time, so every requested percentile gets the same value:

walk = peabiru.travel_time_matrix(
    network, points, points, mode="WALK", percentiles=[75, 25], n_threads=2
)
print(list(walk.columns))

['from_id', 'to_id', 'travel_time_p25', 'travel_time_p75']

Walking with more origins than destinations

When there are more origins than destinations (and no elevation raster), walking trips are routed from the destinations and the columns are swapped back. The two directions can differ on one-way paths; the result still has from_id as the caller's origins.

docs.title: Public transport
docs.text:
mode=["WALK", "TRANSIT"] (or just "TRANSIT") routes by public transport with walking access and egress. A departure_datetime is required; travel times are computed for every departure minute of time_window and summarised by percentiles (up to five, reported in ascending order):

ttm = peabiru.travel_time_matrix(
    network, points, points,
    mode=["WALK", "TRANSIT"],
    departure_datetime=dt.datetime(2019, 5, 13, 14, 0),
    time_window=30,
    percentiles=[5, 50, 95],
    max_trip_duration=20,
    seed=42,
    n_threads=2,
)
print(ttm[ttm["travel_time_p95"].isna()].head(3).to_string())

            from_id            to_id  travel_time_p05  travel_time_p50  travel_time_p95
16  89a8100c007ffff  89a8100c393ffff               19             <NA>             <NA>
44  89a8100c03bffff  89a8100c383ffff               18             <NA>             <NA>
46  89a8100c03bffff  89a8100c15bffff               17               19             <NA>

A pair is reported when its lowest percentile is within max_trip_duration; a higher percentile beyond the limit is missing (<NA>).

docs.title: Transit modes, bicycle and car
docs.text:
Instead of "TRANSIT", mode can name some of the transit modes ("TRAM", "SUBWAY", "RAIL", "BUS", "FERRY", "CABLE_CAR", "GONDOLA", "FUNICULAR"), and its street mode, walking by default, can be "BICYCLE" or "CAR"; mode_egress is the mode from the last stop. A bicycle or car trip to the stops goes on on foot from where the vehicle got, within the same max_bike_time or max_car_time; egress by bicycle or car is limited by max_bike_time or max_car_time (and searched up to 5 km by bicycle or 30 minutes by car):

kw = dict(departure_datetime=dt.datetime(2019, 5, 13, 14, 0), seed=1, n_threads=2)
every = peabiru.travel_time_matrix(network, points, points, mode="TRANSIT", **kw)
bus = peabiru.travel_time_matrix(network, points, points, mode=["WALK", "BUS"], **kw)
bike_car = peabiru.travel_time_matrix(
    network, points, points, mode=["BICYCLE", "TRANSIT"], mode_egress="CAR",
    max_bike_time=10, max_car_time=5, **kw,
)
print([round(float(m["travel_time_p50"].mean()), 2) for m in (every, bus, bike_car)])

[18.03, 19.35, 12.62]

docs.title: Departure times
docs.text:
The date and the clock time of departure_datetime are used as they read: a naive datetime and an aware datetime with the same clock time give the same result, whatever the time zone.

from zoneinfo import ZoneInfo

kw = dict(mode="TRANSIT", seed=1, n_threads=2)
naive = peabiru.travel_time_matrix(
    network, points, points, departure_datetime=dt.datetime(2019, 5, 13, 14, 0), **kw
)
aware = peabiru.travel_time_matrix(
    network, points, points,
    departure_datetime=dt.datetime(2019, 5, 13, 14, 0, tzinfo=ZoneInfo("Asia/Tokyo")),
    **kw,
)
print(naive.equals(aware))

True

docs.title: Frequency-based GTFS and the seed
docs.text:
When a feed describes trips by frequency (frequencies.txt, as the sample feed does), the engine draws draws_per_minute random schedules for each departure minute. Without a seed the result varies from call to call; with a seed it is reproducible.

kw = dict(mode="TRANSIT", departure_datetime=dt.datetime(2019, 5, 13, 14, 0), n_threads=2)
a = peabiru.travel_time_matrix(network, points, points, seed=7, **kw)
b = peabiru.travel_time_matrix(network, points, points, seed=7, **kw)
print(a.equals(b))

True

docs.title: Odd inputs
docs.text:
Points with missing coordinates are not routed (with a warning), and points too far from any street are simply absent from the result. Ids that are not strings are converted with str(), with a warning.

import warnings

odd = pd.concat(
    [
        points.iloc[:3],
        pd.DataFrame({"id": ["no_coords", "far_away"], "lon": [None, 0.0], "lat": [None, 0.0]}),
    ],
    ignore_index=True,
)
with warnings.catch_warnings(record=True) as caught:
    warnings.simplefilter("always")
    m = peabiru.travel_time_matrix(network, odd, points.iloc[:3], mode="WALK", n_threads=2)
print(caught[0].message)
print(sorted(set(m["from_id"])))

1 point(s) in 'origins' have missing lon/lat coordinates and will not be routed. Affected id(s): "no_coords".
['89a8100c007ffff', '89a8100c00fffff', '89a8100c077ffff']

Duplicated ids, a missing id, lon or lat column and non-numeric coordinates are errors.

docs.title: GeoDataFrames
docs.text:
With geopandas installed, origins and destinations can be a GeoDataFrame of points in EPSG:4326 with an id column; the coordinates come from the geometry.

import geopandas as gpd

geo = gpd.GeoDataFrame(
    points[["id", "jobs"]],
    geometry=gpd.points_from_xy(points["lon"], points["lat"]),
    crs="EPSG:4326",
)
from_geo = peabiru.travel_time_matrix(network, geo, geo, mode="CAR", n_threads=2)
print(from_geo.equals(car))

True

docs.title: From long to wide
docs.text:
The result is in long format, one row per pair. A wide origin-by-destination table is one pivot away:

wide = car.pivot(index="from_id", columns="to_id", values="travel_time_p50")
print(wide.iloc[:3, :3])

docs.title: Writing results to files
docs.text:
With output_dir, an existing directory, the result is written there instead of being returned: one CSV file per origin, named from_<origin id>.csv, and the function returns output_dir (a string or a pathlib.Path, as given). The origins are routed a slice at a time and each slice is written before the next one is routed, so a matrix too large to hold in memory can still be computed. accessibility(), expanded_travel_time_matrix() and arrival_travel_time_matrix() take output_dir too.

import tempfile
from pathlib import Path

out = Path(tempfile.mkdtemp())
print(peabiru.travel_time_matrix(network, points, points, mode="CAR",
                                 n_threads=2, output_dir=out) == out)
files = sorted(p.name for p in out.iterdir())
print(len(files), files[0])
print((out / files[0]).read_text().splitlines()[:3])

True
27 from_89a8100c007ffff.csv
['from_id,to_id,travel_time_p50', '89a8100c007ffff,89a8100c00fffff,4', '89a8100c007ffff,89a8100c007ffff,1']

The files hold the columns of the result (accessibility files also keep cutoff under "fixed_exponential", as the placeholder 0), fields holding , or " quoted, a missing value as an empty field, decimals written as in 2.0 and 1.0E-4, lines ended by \n (\r\n on Windows). An origin with no row gets no file (accessibility writes one for every origin). The file names are built from the ids, so an id that cannot name a file in the directory (one with a path separator / or \, or NUL, and on Windows < > : " | ? *) raises ValueError before anything is routed or written. An existing file of the same name is replaced, other files are left alone. "WALK" is then routed from the origins even when there are fewer destinations, and the rule that blanks out trips over max_trip_duration in a returned result is not applied to the files.

docs.title: Threads
docs.text: n_threads=None (the default) uses all cores (math.inf is accepted too). The Python interpreter lock is released while the Rust core routes, so other Python threads keep running.

docs.title: Stopping a long call
docs.text: Ctrl-C stops any of the routing functions within a few tenths of a second and raises KeyboardInterrupt, as it does for Python code; the session stays usable and there is no partial result. Signals reach only Python's main thread, so a call made from another thread runs to the end. build_network() cannot be interrupted.

docs.title: Trip options
docs.text: trip_options() is peabiru's own trip planner: for each origin and destination it gives every trip worth considering, the ones that no other trip beats on all the chosen criteria at once. Where detailed_itineraries() answers "what is the fastest way there?", trip_options() answers "what are my choices?": faster but dearer, cheaper but slower, fewer transfers, less walking.

docs.title: Not dominated
docs.text:
A trip dominates another when it is no worse on every chosen criterion and better on at least one. The criteria are

  • "TIME": door-to-door minutes from the departure minute, waits included;
  • "FARE": the fare by a fare structure (see Fares);
  • "TRANSFERS": rides minus one; a trip without public transport has 0, as many as a trip with a single ride;
  • "WALK": minutes on foot: the access and egress legs when they are walked, and the walks between stops (a bicycle or car leg counts 0).

By default all four are used with a fare structure, all but "FARE" without one. At each departure minute of the window the options are the set of trips not dominated, with one trip per combination of values.

The search is exact, to the second. What is returned is then compared at the resolution the values are read at: total time to a tenth of a minute, as it is reported, and walking to the whole minute (rounded half up; walk_resolution sets the step in seconds, and 1 compares the exact seconds). Of the trips of a minute, one is left out when another is no worse on every criterion in those terms and better on one, or equal on all of them and better in exact terms (less total time, then fewer transfers, less walking, a lower fare). Without this, a trip that is slower, dearer and with more transfers would be returned only because it walks a few seconds less. The values reported stay exact. Rounding cannot make a trip look better than one that beats it to the second, so the result is the same as comparing every trip at that resolution.

The trips follow the rules of the other functions (the same access and egress searches, transfers between stops and boarding rules as detailed_itineraries()), so the times agree with the other functions.

The examples use the sample data of Porto Alegre from the r5r project and its fare structure, downloaded once into the temporary directory, as in the Fares guide.

import datetime as dt
import tempfile
import urllib.request
from pathlib import Path

import pandas as pd

import peabiru

poa = Path(tempfile.gettempdir()) / "peabiru-poa"
poa.mkdir(exist_ok=True)
url = "https://raw.githubusercontent.com/ipea/r5r/v2.5.0/r-package/inst/extdata/poa/"
for name in ["poa_osm.pbf", "poa_eptc.zip", "poa_trensurb.zip", "poa_hexgrid.csv"]:
    if not (poa / name).exists():
        urllib.request.urlretrieve(url + name, poa / name)
fares_zip = Path(tempfile.gettempdir()) / "peabiru-fares_poa.zip"
if not fares_zip.exists():
    urllib.request.urlretrieve(url + "fares/fares_poa.zip", fares_zip)

network = peabiru.build_network(poa)
fares = peabiru.read_fare_structure(fares_zip)
points = pd.read_csv(poa / "poa_hexgrid.csv")
origin = points[points["id"] == "89a90128053ffff"]
destination = points[points["id"] == "89a90129c9bffff"]
departure = dt.datetime(2019, 5, 13, 14, 0)

docs.title: Time and fare
docs.text:
With time and fare as the criteria, the options of this pair over the ten minutes from 14:00 are a ride on the T4 bus, a faster trip with a transfer to the T1D (two fares, with the integration discount: R$ 7.20 instead of R$ 9.60), and walking, which is free:

res = peabiru.trip_options(
    network, origin, destination, departure_datetime=departure,
    criteria=["TIME", "FARE"], fare_structure=fares,
)
cols = ["option", "total_time", "fare", "transfers", "walk_time", "departure_time",
        "n_departures", "description"]
print(res.options[cols].to_string(index=False))

res = peabiru.trip_options(

docs.title: All four criteria and the legs
docs.text:
With the default criteria (all four, here, since there is a fare structure) the trade-offs with transfers and walking come in too. The legs of each option are in itineraries, in the format of detailed_itineraries() and keyed by from_id, to_id and option (a geopandas.GeoDataFrame, or a pandas.DataFrame with drop_geometry=True):

res = peabiru.trip_options(
    network, origin, destination, departure_datetime=departure,
    fare_structure=fares, drop_geometry=True,
)
print(len(res.options), "options")
legs = res.itineraries
print(legs[legs["option"] == 1][["segment", "mode", "cumulative_fare", "segment_duration",
                                 "wait", "distance", "route"]].to_string(index=False))

max_options keeps the first options of each pair, max_fare and max_trip_duration leave out the trips beyond them, and itineraries=False skips the legs.

docs.title: Fares are not additive
docs.text: A fare is not the sum of its rides: a transfer within the time allowance is discounted, some types have unlimited transfers, a cap may apply. Two partial trips are only compared on fare when one is at least as cheap for every way both can continue; the comparison makes no assumption about the fare structure (a discounted transfer may even cost more than two full fares). This exactness has a price: partial trips that could still get a discount are kept apart until they cannot, which makes the fare criterion the slowest one.

docs.title: Frequency-based routes
docs.text:
GTFS frequencies.txt gives a headway, not departure times. The other functions draw random departures (Monte Carlo); trip_options() does not: a frequency-based vehicle is boarded at its expected time, half a headway after the traveller is ready to board (or after the period starts), within the period, and with exact_times = 1 at the first scheduled departure. The results do not change from call to call, and differ on purpose from those draws. The Sao Paulo sample shipped with the package runs by frequency:

spo = peabiru.build_network(peabiru.sample_data_path())
pts = peabiru.sample_points()
res = peabiru.trip_options(
    spo, pts.iloc[[0]], pts.iloc[[26]], departure_datetime=departure,
    time_window=5, itineraries=False,
)
print(res.options[["option", "total_time", "transfers", "walk_time", "n_departures",
                   "description"]].to_string(index=False))

docs.title: Compared with the other functions
docs.text:
• pareto_frontier() gives, for each fare cutoff, the percentiles of the travel time over Monte Carlo draws of departure times: a summary of time against budget, without the trips.
  • detailed_itineraries() gives the fastest trip, or with shortest_path=False the alternatives (one per sequence of routes, the fastest of each).
  • trip_options() gives the trade-offs themselves, trip by trip, with their legs, on any of four criteria. With criteria=["TIME"] and time_window=1, its first option has the total time of detailed_itineraries()'s fastest trip for that minute.
